x.title: Weak lensing and dark energy
x.abstract: We study the power of upcoming weak lensing surveys to probe dark energy. Dark energy modifies the distance-redshift relation as well as the matter power spectrum, both of which affect the weak lensing convergence power spectrum. Some dark-energy models predict additional clustering on very large scales, but this probably cannot be detected by weak lensing alone due to cosmic variance. With reasonable prior information on other cosmological parameters, we find that a survey covering 1000 sq deg down to a limiting magnitude of $R=27$ can impose constraints comparable to those expected from upcoming type Ia supernova and number-count surveys. This result, however, is contingent on the control of both observational and theoretical systematics. Concentrating on the latter, we find that the nonlinear power spectrum of matter perturbations and the redshift distribution of source galaxies both need to be determined accurately in order for weak lensing to achieve its full potential. Finally, we discuss the sensitivity of the three-point statistics to dark energy.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that upcoming weak lensing surveys covering ~1000 sq deg can constrain dark energy with precision comparable to type Ia supernova surveys, provided observational and theoretical systematics are controlled.
tag.dependence_explanation: The weak lensing convergence power spectrum probes the matter distribution, which in the Lambda-CDM framework is dominated by non-baryonic dark matter. The analysis assumes the matter power spectrum and its evolution are governed by dark matter, so rejecting P1 would invalidate the framework used to derive the dark energy constraints.
tag.evidence_quote: Dark energy modifies the distance-redshift relation as well as the matter power spectrum, both of which affect the weak lensing convergence power spectrum.

y.title: The modified Newtonian dynamics—MOND and its implications for new physics
y.abstract: No more salient issue exists in contemporary astrophysics and cosmology than that of the elusive ‘dark matter’. For many years already Milgrom's paradigm of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) has provided an alternative way to interpret observations without appeal to invisible dark matter. MOND had been successful in elucidating economically the dynamics of disc galaxies of all scales, while doing less well for clusters of galaxies; in its original form it could not address gravitational lensing or cosmology. After reviewing some of the evidence in favour of MOND, I recollect the development of relativistic formulations for it to cope with the last deficiency. I comment on recent work by various groups in confronting TeVeS, a relativistic embodiment of MOND, with observational data on gravitational lensing and cosmology. Throughout I ask what sort of physics can be responsible for the efficacy of MOND, and conclude with an appraisal of what theoretical developments are still needed to reach a full description of the world involving no unobserved matter.

tag.main_claim: The author reviews MOND as a viable alternative to dark matter for explaining galaxy dynamics, with its relativistic formulation TeVeS extending the framework to gravitational lensing and cosmology, though further theoretical development is still needed for a complete dark-matter-free description.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's central thesis is that galaxy dynamics can be explained without dark matter (Q1) via modified dynamics at low accelerations (Q2), and it highlights MOND's success in economically elucidating disc galaxy dynamics including scaling relations (Q3). If any of these were false, the paper's argument for MOND as a viable alternative framework would collapse.
tag.evidence_quote: Milgrom's paradigm of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) has provided an alternative way to interpret observations without appeal to invisible dark matter. MOND had been successful in elucidating economically the dynamics of disc galaxies of all scales

judge.conjunction: Upcoming weak lensing surveys can constrain dark energy with precision comparable to type Ia supernova surveys, provided systematics are controlled [x], while MOND offers a viable dark-matter-free explanation of galaxy dynamics, extended to lensing and cosmology via TeVeS [y].
judge.x_background_statement: The weak lensing convergence power spectrum probes the total matter power spectrum, which in the standard cosmological framework is dominated by non-baryonic dark matter; dark-energy constraints are derived within this Lambda-CDM framework.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone, without non-baryonic dark matter, and MOND/TeVeS provides a complete description of lensing and cosmology on this basis.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: If galaxy dynamics and lensing are explained by baryonic matter alone without dark matter (Q1), then the matter power spectrum is not dominated by non-baryonic dark matter (P1), and the standard weak-lensing forecast methodology of paper x—which treats the matter power spectrum as dark-matter-dominated—would be invalid or require fundamental reformulation.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Weak lensing surveys can precisely constrain dark energy through the dark-matter-dominated matter power spectrum, while MOND correctly explains galaxy dynamics without dark matter, together offering a complete and self-consistent account of cosmological observations across all scales.
judge.notes: The dependence of X on P1 is indirect: paper x is about dark *energy* constraints, not dark *matter* per se, but the entire forecasting methodology assumes the Lambda-CDM matter power spectrum dominated by non-baryonic dark matter. Paper y explicitly extends TeVeS to lensing and cosmology, so the two frameworks overlap on the domain of gravitational lensing—the regime separation is not clean. The orphan conclusion is real but somewhat abstract; a reviewer might argue that a careful writer could scope each claim to its respective framework. The key tension is that paper x's weak-lensing analysis requires dark matter to dominate the matter power spectrum, while paper y's framework denies dark matter exists at all, making the conjunction's implicit assumption—that both results can be used simultaneously—unwarranted.

x.title: Substructure and Halo Density Profiles in a Warm Dark Matter Cosmology
x.abstract: We performed a series of high-resolution collisionless N -body simulations designed to study the substructure of Milky Way-size galactic halos (host halos) and the density profiles of halos in a warm dark matter (WDM) scenario with a nonvanishing cosmological constant. The virial masses of the host halos range from 3.5 × 10 12 to 1.7 × 10 12 h -1 M ☉ , and they have more than 10 5 particles each. A key feature of the WDM power spectrum is the free-streaming length R f ,WDM , which fixes an additional parameter for the model of structure formation. We analyze the substructure of host halos using three R f ,WDM values: 0.2, 0.1, and 0.05 Mpc, and compare results to the predictions of the cold dark matter (CDM) model. We find that guest halos (satellites) do form in the WDM scenario, but are more easily destroyed by dynamical friction and tidal disruption than their counterparts in a CDM model. The small number of guest halos that we find in the WDM models with respect to the CDM one is the result of a lower guest halo accretion and a higher satellite destruction rate. These two phenomena operate almost with the same intensity in delivering a reduced number of guest halos at z = 0. For the model with R f ,WDM = 0.1 Mpc, the number of accreted small halos is a factor of 2.5 below that of the CDM model, while the fraction of destroyed satellites is almost twice as large as that of the CDM model. The larger the R f ,WDM value, the greater the size of these two effects and the smaller the abundance of satellites. Under the assumption that each guest halo hosts a luminous galaxy, we find that the observed circular velocity function of satellites around the Milky Way and Andromeda is well described by the R f ,WDM = 0.1 Mpc WDM model. In the R f ,WDM = 0.1-0.2 Mpc models, the surviving guest halos at z = 0, whose masses are in the range M h ≈ 10 9 -10 11 h -1 M ☉ , have an average concentration parameter c 1/5 = r ( M h )/ r ( M h /5), which is approximately twice as small as that of the corresponding CDM guest halos. This difference very likely produces the higher satellite destruction rate found in the WDM models. The density profile of host halos is well described by the Navarro, Frenk, & White (NFW) fit, whereas guest halos show a wide variety of density profiles. A tendency to form shallow cores is not evident; the profiles, however, are limited by a poor mass resolution in the innermost regions where shallow cores could be expected.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that warm dark matter models with a free-streaming length of 0.1 Mpc produce fewer satellite halos than CDM through reduced accretion and enhanced tidal destruction, matching the observed satellite circular velocity function of the Milky Way and Andromeda.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire simulation framework assumes non-baryonic dark matter dominates halo masses (P1), uses Newtonian dynamics for N-body evolution (P2), and treats halos as collisionless dark matter structures (P4). Rejecting any of these would eliminate the basis for the simulation predictions about satellite substructure.
tag.evidence_quote: We performed a series of high-resolution collisionless N-body simulations designed to study the substructure of Milky Way-size galactic halos (host halos) and the density profiles of halos in a warm dark matter (WDM) scenario with a nonvanishing cosmological constant.

y.title: ANDROMEDA DWARFS IN LIGHT OF MODIFIED NEWTONIAN DYNAMICS
y.abstract: We compare the recently published velocity dispersions for 17 Andromeda dwarf spheroidals with estimates of the modified Newtonian dynamics predictions, based on the luminosities of these dwarfs, with reasonable stellar mass-to-light values and no dark matter. We find that the two are consistent within the uncertainties. We further predict the velocity dispersions of another 10 dwarfs for which only photometric data are currently available.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that MOND predictions based on baryonic mass alone (with no dark matter) are consistent with observed velocity dispersions of Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxies.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper tests whether dwarf galaxy dynamics can be explained by baryonic matter alone without dark matter (Q1), using MOND's modified force law that breaks from Newtonian dynamics at low accelerations (Q2) and produces scaling predictions directly from that law (Q3). If any of these were rejected, the predicted velocity dispersions would not be valid comparisons.
tag.evidence_quote: We compare the recently published velocity dispersions for 17 Andromeda dwarf spheroidals with estimates of the modified Newtonian dynamics predictions, based on the luminosities of these dwarfs, with reasonable stellar mass-to-light values and no dark matter. We find that the two are consistent within the uncertainties.

judge.conjunction: Studies of the Andromeda satellite system have shown that warm dark matter models with a free-streaming length of 0.1 Mpc reproduce the observed satellite circular velocity function [x], while MOND predictions based on baryonic mass alone are consistent with the observed velocity dispersions of Andromeda dwarf spheroidals [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Milky Way-size galaxies are surrounded by dark matter halos containing collisionless substructure whose properties govern the observed satellite galaxy population.
judge.y_background_statement: The dynamics of Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxies are governed by modified Newtonian dynamics applied to baryonic mass alone, with no dark matter halos.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: X requires that dark matter halos exist and their substructure governs satellite galaxy properties; Y requires that no dark matter exists and galaxy dynamics are explained by baryons alone under MOND. These are mutually exclusive ontological commitments about the nature of matter in galactic systems.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Both warm dark matter substructure and MOND baryonic-only dynamics simultaneously and successfully describe the Andromeda satellite system, implying that both the dark matter paradigm and the no-dark-matter paradigm are valid descriptions of the same phenomenon.
judge.notes: Both papers study the Andromeda satellite/dwarf galaxy system but from fundamentally incompatible paradigms. Paper x simulates WDM halo substructure within the dark matter framework; paper y predicts velocity dispersions without dark matter using MOND. The conjunction appears superficially compatible because X addresses the satellite circular velocity function (a population-level statistic) while Y addresses individual galaxy velocity dispersions, but both make claims about the same physical system with contradictory assumptions about whether dark matter exists. A human verifier should confirm that the observational quantities (circular velocity function vs. velocity dispersions) are not easily separable into distinct regimes, since both ultimately probe the gravitational dynamics of the same dwarf galaxies.

x.title: ΛCDM is Consistent with SPARC Radial Acceleration Relation
x.abstract: Abstract Recent analysis of the Spitzer Photometry and Accurate Rotation Curve (SPARC) galaxy sample found a surprisingly tight relation between the radial acceleration inferred from the rotation curves and the acceleration due to the baryonic components of the disk. It has been suggested that this relation may be evidence for new physics, beyond ΛCDM. In this Letter, we show that 32 galaxies from the MUGS2 match the SPARC acceleration relation. These cosmological simulations of star-forming, rotationally supported disks were simulated with a WMAP3 ΛCDM cosmology, and match the SPARC acceleration relation with less scatter than the observational data. These results show that this acceleration relation is a consequence of dissipative collapse of baryons, rather than being evidence for exotic dark-sector physics or new dynamical laws.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the SPARC radial acceleration relation arises naturally from dissipative collapse of baryons in ΛCDM simulations, rather than requiring modified dynamics or new fundamental laws.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim relies on P1 because the simulations are ΛCDM cosmological simulations with dark matter halos; without dark matter the simulation setup is invalid. It relies on P2 because the simulations use Newtonian gravity, so if dynamics break down at low accelerations the simulated relation would be meaningless. It directly asserts P3, that the radial acceleration relation emerges from galaxy formation physics rather than being a fundamental law.
tag.evidence_quote: These cosmological simulations of star-forming, rotationally supported disks were simulated with a WMAP3 ΛCDM cosmology, and match the SPARC acceleration relation with less scatter than the observational data. These results show that this acceleration relation is a consequence of dissipative collapse of baryons, rather than being evidence for exotic dark-sector physics or new dynamical laws.

y.title: MOND laws of galactic dynamics
y.abstract: Modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) predicts a number of laws that galactic systems should obey irrespective of their complicated, haphazard and mostly unknowable histories – as Kepler's laws are obeyed by planetary systems. The main purpose of this work is to show how, and to what extent, these MOND laws follow from only the paradigm's basic tenets: departure from standard dynamics at accelerations a ≲ a0 and space–time scale invariance in the limit a ≪ a0. Such predictions will be shared by all MOND theories that embody these premises. This is important because we do not know which of the existing MOND theories, if any, is a step in the right direction. In the Newtonian dynamics plus dark matter paradigm, the validity of such clear-cut laws – which tightly constrain baryons, ‘dark matter’ and their mutual relations – is contrary to expectations.

tag.main_claim: Milgrom shows that MOND predicts clear-cut laws of galactic dynamics that follow directly from the paradigm's basic tenets—modified dynamics at low accelerations and space-time scale invariance—akin to how Kepler's laws follow from Newtonian gravity.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's claim that galactic dynamical laws follow from MOND tenets requires that galaxy dynamics be explained without dark matter (Q1), that Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2, explicitly cited as a basic tenet), and that scaling relations derive from the force law rather than from galaxy formation (Q3).
tag.evidence_quote: The main purpose of this work is to show how, and to what extent, these MOND laws follow from only the paradigm's basic tenets: departure from standard dynamics at accelerations a ≲ a0 and space–time scale invariance in the limit a ≪ a0.

judge.conjunction: The SPARC radial acceleration relation arises naturally from dissipative collapse of baryons in ΛCDM simulations, rather than requiring modified dynamics or new fundamental laws [x], and MOND predicts clear-cut laws of galactic dynamics that follow directly from its basic tenets of modified dynamics at low accelerations and space-time scale invariance [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Most matter in the universe is non-baryonic dark matter, and the radial acceleration relation is a consequence of galaxy formation within dark matter halos, not a fundamental law.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone without dark matter, and scaling relations like the radial acceleration relation follow directly from the modified force law.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 posits that galaxies are embedded in non-baryonic dark matter halos, while Q1 posits that galaxy dynamics are fully explained by baryonic matter alone with no dark matter. These are mutually exclusive ontological commitments about the matter content of galaxies.
judge.notes: Paper x's claim X explicitly states the radial acceleration relation arises 'rather than requiring modified dynamics or new fundamental laws,' directly contradicting paper y's claim Y that MOND's modified dynamics predict these laws. The conflict is on the surface: X denies the very mechanism (modified dynamics) that Y affirms. This is a direct competing-explanations case, not a hidden theoretical conflict. A human verifier should confirm that the 'rather than' clause in X makes the surface inconsistency explicit.

x.title: Weak‐Lensing Mass Reconstruction of the Interacting Cluster 1E 0657−558: Direct Evidence for the Existence of Dark Matter
x.abstract: We present a weak-lensing mass reconstruction of the interacting cluster 1E 0657-558, in which we detect both the main cluster and a subcluster. The subcluster is identified as a smaller cluster that has just undergone initial infall and pass-through of the primary cluster and has been previously identified in both optical surveys and X-ray studies. The X-ray gas has been separated from the galaxies by ram pressure-stripping during the pass-through. The detected mass peak is located between the X-ray peak and galaxy concentration, although the position is consistent with the galaxy centroid within the errors of the mass reconstruction. We find that the mass peak for the main cluster is in good spatial agreement with the cluster galaxies and is offset from the X-ray halo at 3.4 σ significance, and we determine that the mass-to-light ratios of the two components are consistent with those of relaxed clusters. The observed offsets of the lensing mass peaks from the peaks of the dominant visible mass component (the X-ray gas) directly demonstrate the presence, and dominance, of dark matter in this cluster. This proof of dark matter existence holds true even under the assumption of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND); based on the observed gravitational shear-optical light ratios and the mass peak-X-ray gas offsets, the dark matter component in a MOND regime would have a total mass that is at least equal to the baryonic mass of the system.

tag.main_claim: Clowe et al. show that the offset between weak-lensing mass peaks and X-ray gas peaks in the Bullet Cluster (1E 0657−558) directly demonstrates the existence and dominance of dark matter, even under MOND assumptions.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim that the mass–baryon offset proves the existence of dark matter requires that non-baryonic dark matter is a real constituent of the universe (P1) and that cluster lensing mass is dominated by collisionless dark matter rather than modified gravity (P4). If cluster mass discrepancies were instead due to modified gravity (Q4), the spatial offset would not demonstrate dark matter.
tag.evidence_quote: The observed offsets of the lensing mass peaks from the peaks of the dominant visible mass component (the X-ray gas) directly demonstrate the presence, and dominance, of dark matter in this cluster. This proof of dark matter existence holds true even under the assumption of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND); based on the observed gravitational shear-optical light ratios and the mass peak-X-ray gas offsets, the dark matter component in a MOND regime would have a total mass that is at least equal to the baryonic mass of the system.

y.title: Can MOND take a bullet? Analytical comparisons of three versions of MOND beyond spherical symmetry
y.abstract: A proper test of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) in systems of non-trivial geometries depends on modelling subtle differences in several versions of its postulated theories. This is especially true for lensing and dynamics of barely virialized galaxy clusters with typical gravity of scale a0. The original MOND formula, the classical single-field modification of the Poisson equation, and the multifield general relativistic theory of Bekenstein (tensor–vector–scalar, TeVeS) all lead to different predictions as we stray from spherical symmetry. In this paper, we study a class of analytical MONDian models for a system with a semi-Hernquist baryonic profile. After presenting the analytical distribution function of the baryons in spherical limits, we develop orbits and gravitational lensing of the models in non-spherical geometries. In particular, we can generate a multicentred baryonic system with a weak lensing signal resembling that of the merging galaxy cluster 1E 0657−56 with a bullet-like light distribution. We finally present analytical scale-free highly non-spherical models to show the subtle differences between the single-field classical MOND theory and the multifield TeVeS theory.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that different versions of MOND theory (original formula, single-field Poisson modification, and TeVeS) yield different predictions in non-spherical geometries, and that MONDian baryonic models can reproduce a weak lensing signal resembling the Bullet Cluster (1E 0657−56).
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper works entirely within the MOND framework: it assumes baryonic matter alone drives the gravitational field (Q1), that dynamics are governed by modified gravity at acceleration scale a0 (Q2), and that cluster lensing signals arise from modified gravity rather than dark matter (Q4). If any of these were rejected, the exercise of modeling the Bullet Cluster with baryonic profiles under MOND would be unmotivated.
tag.evidence_quote: This is especially true for lensing and dynamics of barely virialized galaxy clusters with typical gravity of scale a0. ... we can generate a multicentred baryonic system with a weak lensing signal resembling that of the merging galaxy cluster 1E 0657−56 with a bullet-like light distribution.

judge.conjunction: The Bullet Cluster's weak-lensing mass reconstruction directly demonstrates the existence and dominance of dark matter even under MOND assumptions [x], and analytical MONDian baryonic models in non-spherical geometries can reproduce a weak lensing signal resembling the Bullet Cluster [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Most matter in the universe is non-baryonic dark matter, and the Bullet Cluster's mass-to-light ratios and mass-gas offsets require a collisionless dark matter component even if MOND replaces Newtonian dynamics.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy and cluster dynamics can be explained by baryonic matter alone under modified gravity, without any non-baryonic dark matter component.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 requires a non-baryonic dark matter component to explain the Bullet Cluster observations even under MOND, while Q1 holds that baryonic matter alone under modified gravity suffices to reproduce the same weak lensing signal. The two positions cannot both be true of the same system.
judge.notes: The two tagged claims directly conflict on their face. Paper x concludes that dark matter is required even under MOND to explain the Bullet Cluster's lensing and mass-gas offsets. Paper y concludes that MONDian baryonic models alone can reproduce a weak lensing signal resembling the Bullet Cluster. These are competing conclusions about the same observational system, not compatible claims whose conflict is hidden in background theory. A literature review citing both would necessarily present them as opposing viewpoints, not as jointly true. The hidden-conflict pattern requires surface-level compatibility; that condition fails here.

x.title: Weak‐Lensing Mass Reconstruction of the Interacting Cluster 1E 0657−558: Direct Evidence for the Existence of Dark Matter
x.abstract: We present a weak-lensing mass reconstruction of the interacting cluster 1E 0657-558, in which we detect both the main cluster and a subcluster. The subcluster is identified as a smaller cluster that has just undergone initial infall and pass-through of the primary cluster and has been previously identified in both optical surveys and X-ray studies. The X-ray gas has been separated from the galaxies by ram pressure-stripping during the pass-through. The detected mass peak is located between the X-ray peak and galaxy concentration, although the position is consistent with the galaxy centroid within the errors of the mass reconstruction. We find that the mass peak for the main cluster is in good spatial agreement with the cluster galaxies and is offset from the X-ray halo at 3.4 σ significance, and we determine that the mass-to-light ratios of the two components are consistent with those of relaxed clusters. The observed offsets of the lensing mass peaks from the peaks of the dominant visible mass component (the X-ray gas) directly demonstrate the presence, and dominance, of dark matter in this cluster. This proof of dark matter existence holds true even under the assumption of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND); based on the observed gravitational shear-optical light ratios and the mass peak-X-ray gas offsets, the dark matter component in a MOND regime would have a total mass that is at least equal to the baryonic mass of the system.

tag.main_claim: Clowe et al. show that the offset between weak-lensing mass peaks and X-ray gas peaks in the Bullet Cluster (1E 0657−558) directly demonstrates the existence and dominance of dark matter, even under MOND assumptions.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim that the mass–baryon offset proves the existence of dark matter requires that non-baryonic dark matter is a real constituent of the universe (P1) and that cluster lensing mass is dominated by collisionless dark matter rather than modified gravity (P4). If cluster mass discrepancies were instead due to modified gravity (Q4), the spatial offset would not demonstrate dark matter.
tag.evidence_quote: The observed offsets of the lensing mass peaks from the peaks of the dominant visible mass component (the X-ray gas) directly demonstrate the presence, and dominance, of dark matter in this cluster. This proof of dark matter existence holds true even under the assumption of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND); based on the observed gravitational shear-optical light ratios and the mass peak-X-ray gas offsets, the dark matter component in a MOND regime would have a total mass that is at least equal to the baryonic mass of the system.

y.title: Can MOND take a bullet? Analytical comparisons of three versions of MOND beyond spherical symmetry
y.abstract: A proper test of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) in systems of non-trivial geometries depends on modelling subtle differences in several versions of its postulated theories. This is especially true for lensing and dynamics of barely virialized galaxy clusters with typical gravity of scale a0. The original MOND formula, the classical single-field modification of the Poisson equation, and the multifield general relativistic theory of Bekenstein (tensor–vector–scalar, TeVeS) all lead to different predictions as we stray from spherical symmetry. In this paper, we study a class of analytical MONDian models for a system with a semi-Hernquist baryonic profile. After presenting the analytical distribution function of the baryons in spherical limits, we develop orbits and gravitational lensing of the models in non-spherical geometries. In particular, we can generate a multicentred baryonic system with a weak lensing signal resembling that of the merging galaxy cluster 1E 0657−56 with a bullet-like light distribution. We finally present analytical scale-free highly non-spherical models to show the subtle differences between the single-field classical MOND theory and the multifield TeVeS theory.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that different versions of MOND theory (original formula, single-field Poisson modification, and TeVeS) yield different predictions in non-spherical geometries, and that MONDian baryonic models can reproduce a weak lensing signal resembling the Bullet Cluster (1E 0657−56).
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper works entirely within the MOND framework: it assumes baryonic matter alone drives the gravitational field (Q1), that dynamics are governed by modified gravity at acceleration scale a0 (Q2), and that cluster lensing signals arise from modified gravity rather than dark matter (Q4). If any of these were rejected, the exercise of modeling the Bullet Cluster with baryonic profiles under MOND would be unmotivated.
tag.evidence_quote: This is especially true for lensing and dynamics of barely virialized galaxy clusters with typical gravity of scale a0. ... we can generate a multicentred baryonic system with a weak lensing signal resembling that of the merging galaxy cluster 1E 0657−56 with a bullet-like light distribution.

judge.conjunction: Studies of the Bullet Cluster provide direct evidence for the existence and dominance of dark matter even under MOND assumptions [x], while MONDian baryonic models can reproduce weak lensing signals resembling this system in non-spherical geometries [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Galaxy clusters and lensing mass are dominated by collisionless dark matter (P4).
judge.y_background_statement: The mass discrepancy in galaxy clusters reflects modified gravity (plus missing baryons), not collisionless dark matter (Q4).
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P4 asserts that cluster lensing mass is dominated by collisionless dark matter, while Q4 asserts that the mass discrepancy in clusters reflects modified gravity rather than collisionless dark matter. These are mutually exclusive explanations of the same lensing observations.
judge.orphan_conclusion: The Bullet Cluster's lensing signal is explained by a combination of modified gravity effects and a dark matter component, where both MOND and dark matter contribute to the observed mass discrepancy.
judge.notes: Both papers study the same system (1E 0657-558/56, the Bullet Cluster). Paper x explicitly argues dark matter is needed even under MOND, while paper y shows MOND baryonic models can produce similar lensing signals. The hybrid conclusion (MOND + dark matter both contribute) is rejected by pure ΛCDM (P2: Newtonian dynamics hold, no modification needed) and by pure MOND (Q1: no dark matter). A verifier should check whether paper y's models reproduce the specific mass peak–X-ray gas offset that paper x uses as its key 3.4σ evidence, or merely produce a superficially similar weak-lensing morphology without matching that critical diagnostic.

x.title: Mapping the dark matter with weak gravitational lensing
x.abstract: We consider the problem of reconstructing the projected mass distribution in clusters from coherent distortions of background galaxies. The ellipticity of a background galaxy provides an estimate of the trace-free components of the tidal field {second partial derivative of {PHI} with respect to θ_i_, θ_j_} where {PHI}(θ) is the two-dimensional potential generated by the surface density {SIGMA}(θ). We present a technique for inverting this problem. The resulting surface density contains a strong, but incoherent, random component arising from the random intrinsic galaxy ellipticities. This can be removed by filtering. Our method is very similar in form to that of Tyson et al., and the latter is given a rigorous interpretation as a particular implementation of filtering. We present simulations to illustrate the application of the method.

tag.main_claim: Kaiser & Squires show that the projected mass distribution in galaxy clusters can be reconstructed from coherent distortions of background galaxies via weak gravitational lensing.
tag.dependence_explanation: The reconstruction method assumes the standard Poisson equation relating surface density to gravitational potential (P2), since it inverts lensing distortions into a mass map using standard gravity. The paper's explicit purpose is to map dark matter in clusters (P4), so if clusters are not dark-matter-dominated the central goal and interpretation of the reconstructed map is undercut.
tag.evidence_quote: We consider the problem of reconstructing the projected mass distribution in clusters from coherent distortions of background galaxies. The ellipticity of a background galaxy provides an estimate of the trace-free components of the tidal field {second partial derivative of {PHI} with respect to θ_i_, θ_j_} where {PHI}(θ) is the two-dimensional potential generated by the surface density {SIGMA}(θ).

y.title: Testing the MOND Paradigm of Modified Dynamics with Galaxy-Galaxy Gravitational Lensing
y.abstract: The MOND paradigm of modified dynamics predicts that the asymptotic gravitational potential of an isolated, bounded (baryonic) mass, $M$, is $\ensuremath{\phi}(r)=(MG{a}_{0}{)}^{1/2}\mathrm{ln}﻿(r)$. Relativistic MOND theories predict that the lensing effects of $M$ are dictated by $\ensuremath{\phi}(r)$ as general-relativity lensing is dictated by the Newtonian potential. Thus MOND predicts that the asymptotic Newtonian potential deduced from galaxy-galaxy gravitational lensing will have (1) a logarithmic $r$ dependence, and (2) a normalization (parametrized standardly as $2{\ensuremath{\sigma}}^{2}$) that depends only on $M$: $\ensuremath{\sigma}=(MG{a}_{0}/4{)}^{1/4}$. I compare these predictions with recent results of galaxy-galaxy lensing, and find agreement on all counts. For the ``blue''-lenses subsample (``spiral'' galaxies) MOND reproduces the observations well with an ${r}^{\ensuremath{'}}$-band $M/{L}_{{r}^{\ensuremath{'}}}\ensuremath{\sim}(1--3)(M/L{)}_{\ensuremath{\bigodot}}$, and for ``red'' lenses (``elliptical'' galaxies) with $M/{L}_{{r}^{\ensuremath{'}}}\ensuremath{\sim}(3--6)(M/L{)}_{\ensuremath{\bigodot}}$, both consistent with baryons only. In contradistinction, Newtonian analysis requires, typically, $M/{L}_{{r}^{\ensuremath{'}}}\ensuremath{\sim}130(M/L{)}_{\ensuremath{\bigodot}}$, bespeaking a mass discrepancy of a factor $\ensuremath{\sim}40$. Compared with the staple, rotation-curve tests, MOND is here tested in a wider population of galaxies, through a different phenomenon, using relativistic test objects, and is probed to several-times-lower accelerations--as low as a few percent of ${a}_{0}$.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that MOND's predictions for galaxy-galaxy gravitational lensing—a logarithmic radial potential and a normalization σ = (MGa₀/4)^(1/4)—are confirmed by observations using baryonic mass-to-light ratios, while Newtonian analysis requires a mass discrepancy factor of ~40.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim requires that Newtonian dynamics break down below a₀ (Q2), producing the predicted logarithmic potential and σ scaling relation directly from the modified force law (Q3), and that the observed lensing is explained by baryonic matter alone without dark matter (Q1). Rejecting any of these would undercut the conclusion that MOND succeeds where dark-matter analysis fails.
tag.evidence_quote: The MOND paradigm of modified dynamics predicts that the asymptotic gravitational potential of an isolated, bounded (baryonic) mass, M, is φ(r)=(MGa0)^(1/2)ln(r)... σ=(MGa0/4)^(1/4). I compare these predictions with recent results of galaxy-galaxy lensing, and find agreement on all counts... both consistent with baryons only.

judge.conjunction: Weak gravitational lensing enables reconstruction of the projected mass distribution in galaxy clusters [x], and galaxy-galaxy lensing observations confirm MOND's predicted logarithmic potential with baryons-only mass-to-light ratios [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Gravitational lensing deflections are governed by the standard GR/Newtonian gravitational potential at all accelerations, so the reconstructed surface mass density reflects the true mass distribution including any dark matter.
judge.y_background_statement: Newtonian dynamics break down below a0, causing the gravitational potential to take a logarithmic asymptotic form, so the mass discrepancy inferred from standard Newtonian lensing analysis is an artifact of using invalid dynamics rather than evidence for dark matter.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: If GR/Newtonian dynamics hold at low accelerations (P2), the Kaiser & Squires lensing reconstruction yields true mass distributions and any mass discrepancy is real dark matter. If Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2), the standard lensing equations are invalid in that regime and the 'mass' they reconstruct is partly an artifact of modified gravity rather than real matter.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Weak-lensing mass maps reveal the true dark matter distribution in galaxy clusters, while the same lensing phenomenon applied to individual galaxies reveals no dark matter but instead confirms that Newtonian dynamics fail at low accelerations.
judge.notes: Paper x is a method paper that does not explicitly invoke dark matter or low accelerations, but its lensing inversion is derived within standard GR and would yield spurious mass if Q2 holds. Paper y explicitly shows Newtonian lensing analysis produces a factor ~40 mass discrepancy that vanishes under MOND. The orphan conclusion is incoherent because if MOND is correct, cluster lensing mass maps are also artifacts of invalid Newtonian analysis, not true mass distributions—so one cannot simultaneously accept cluster mass maps as real dark matter and galaxy lensing as baryons-only. A human verifier should check whether MOND's known cluster-scale shortcomings (where even MOND needs extra mass) could provide a partial regime separation, but the fundamental P2 vs Q2 conflict applies to both regimes.

x.title: Radial Acceleration Relation of ΛCDM Satellite Galaxies
x.abstract: The radial acceleration measured in bright galaxies tightly correlates with that generated by the observed distribution of baryons, a phenomenon known as the radial acceleration relation (RAR). Dwarf spheroidal satellite galaxies have been recently found to depart from the extrapolation of the RAR measured for more massive objects but with a substantially larger scatter. If confirmed by new data, this result provides a powerful test of the theory of gravity at low accelerations that requires robust theoretical predictions. By using high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations, we show that, within the standard model of cosmology (ΛCDM), satellite galaxies are expected to follow the same RAR as brighter systems but with a much larger scatter which does not correlate with the physical properties of the galaxies. In the simulations, the RAR evolves mildly with redshift. Moreover, the acceleration due to the gravitational field of the host has no effect on the RAR. This is in contrast with the external field effect in modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) which causes galaxies in strong external fields to deviate from the RAR. This difference between ΛCDM and MOND offers a possible way to discriminate between them.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that within ΛCDM simulations, satellite galaxies follow the same radial acceleration relation as brighter systems but with larger scatter, and the host's gravitational field has no effect on the RAR, in contrast with MOND's external field effect.
tag.dependence_explanation: The simulations are built on ΛCDM with dark matter halos (P1) and Newtonian gravity (P2), and the central result is that the RAR emerges from galaxy formation processes rather than a fundamental law (P3). The key discriminant—that no external field effect exists—requires that Newtonian dynamics hold at low accelerations (P2), since MOND's external field effect is a direct consequence of dynamics breaking down below a0.
tag.evidence_quote: By using high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations, we show that, within the standard model of cosmology (ΛCDM), satellite galaxies are expected to follow the same RAR as brighter systems but with a much larger scatter which does not correlate with the physical properties of the galaxies. Moreover, the acceleration due to the gravitational field of the host has no effect on the RAR. This is in contrast with the external field effect in modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) which causes galaxies in strong external fields to deviate from the RAR.

y.title: Testing the Strong Equivalence Principle. II. Relating the External Field Effect in Galaxy Rotation Curves to the Large-scale Structure of the Universe
y.abstract: Abstract Theories of modified gravity generically violate the strong equivalence principle, so that the internal dynamics of a self-gravitating system in freefall depends on the strength of the external gravitational field (the external field effect). We fit rotation curves (RCs) from the SPARC database with a model inspired by Milgromian dynamics (MOND), which relates the outer shape of an RC to the external Newtonian field from the large-scale baryonic matter distribution through a dimensionless parameter e N. We obtain a > 4σ statistical detection of the external field effect (i.e. e N > 0 on average), confirming previous results. We then locate the SPARC galaxies in the cosmic web of the nearby universe and find a striking contrast in the fitted e N values for galaxies in underdense versus overdense regions. Galaxies in an underdense region between 22 and 45 Mpc from the celestial axis in the northern sky have RC fits consistent with e N ≃ 0, while those in overdense regions adjacent to the CfA2 Great Wall and the Perseus−Pisces Supercluster return e N that are a factor of two larger than the median for SPARC galaxies. We also calculate independent estimates of e N from galaxy survey data and find that they agree with the e N inferred from the RCs within the uncertainties, the chief uncertainty being the spatial distribution of baryons not contained in galaxies or clusters.

tag.main_claim: Chae et al. detect the external field effect in galaxy rotation curves at >4σ significance, showing that internal galactic dynamics depend on the external gravitational field from large-scale baryonic matter, consistent with MOND.
tag.dependence_explanation: The external field effect exists only when Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2), making internal dynamics of a self-gravitating system depend on the external field strength. The model also assumes the external field is sourced by baryonic matter alone (Q1); if dark matter dominated the gravitational field (P1), the baryonic-based external field estimates would be invalid and the EFE would not arise.
tag.evidence_quote: Theories of modified gravity generically violate the strong equivalence principle, so that the internal dynamics of a self-gravitating system in freefall depends on the strength of the external gravitational field (the external field effect). We fit rotation curves (RCs) from the SPARC database with a model inspired by Milgromian dynamics (MOND), which relates the outer shape of an RC to the external Newtonian field from the large-scale baryonic matter distribution through a dimensionless parameter e N.

judge.conjunction: The radial acceleration relation has been examined both theoretically and observationally: ΛCDM simulations predict that satellite galaxies follow the RAR with larger scatter and no host-field effect, in contrast with MOND [x], while observations of galaxy rotation curves detect the external field effect at >4σ significance, consistent with MOND [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Most matter in the universe is non-baryonic dark matter, and galaxy dynamics are governed by Newtonian/GR gravity with dark matter halos (ΛCDM).
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone without dark matter, under a modified force law that violates the strong equivalence principle (MOND).
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 posits that non-baryonic dark matter is the dominant mass component driving galaxy dynamics, while Q1 explicitly excludes dark matter and attributes all galactic dynamics to baryonic matter under modified gravity.
judge.notes: The two papers address the same physical phenomenon—the external field effect—and reach directly opposite conclusions. Paper x explicitly states that ΛCDM predicts no host-field effect and contrasts this with MOND's external field effect. Paper y reports a >4σ detection of exactly that effect and frames it as consistent with MOND. Both papers explicitly position the external field effect as a discriminator between ΛCDM and MOND. The conflict is on the surface, not hidden in background theory; a writer citing both as if compatible would be citing contradictory empirical results, not overlooking a subtle theoretical incompatibility.

x.title: Testing phenomenological and theoretical models of dark matter density profiles with galaxy clusters
x.abstract: We use the stacked gravitational lensing mass profile of four high-mass (M >~10^{15}Msun) galaxy clusters around z ~ 0.3 from Umetsu et al. to fit density profiles of phenomenological [Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW), Einasto, Sérsic, Stadel, Baltz-Marshall-Oguri (BMO) and Hernquist] and theoretical (non-singular Isothermal Sphere, DARKexp and Kang & He) models of the dark matter distribution. We account for large-scale structure effects, including a 2-halo term in the analysis. We find that the BMO model provides the best fit to the data as measured by the reduced chi^2. It is followed by the Stadel profile, the generalized NFW profile with a free inner slope and by the Einasto profile. The NFW model provides the best fit if we neglect the 2-halo term, in agreement with results from Umetsu et al. Among the theoretical profiles, the DARKexp model with a single form parameter has the best performance, very close to that of the BMO profile. This may indicate a connection between this theoretical model and the phenomenology of dark matter halos, shedding light on the dynamical basis of empirical profiles which emerge from numerical simulations.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the BMO dark matter density profile provides the best fit to stacked galaxy cluster lensing mass profiles, with the DARKexp theoretical model performing comparably well, among several phenomenological and theoretical dark matter halo models.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis fits dark matter density profiles to gravitational lensing mass profiles of galaxy clusters, which requires that cluster lensing mass is dominated by collisionless dark matter (P4) and that most matter is non-baryonic dark matter (P1). Without these assumptions, modeling the lensing signal as a dark matter distribution would be meaningless.
tag.evidence_quote: We use the stacked gravitational lensing mass profile of four high-mass (M >~10^{15}Msun) galaxy clusters around z ~ 0.3 from Umetsu et al. to fit density profiles of phenomenological [Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW), Einasto, Sérsic, Stadel, Baltz-Marshall-Oguri (BMO) and Hernquist] and theoretical (non-singular Isothermal Sphere, DARKexp and Kang & He) models of the dark matter distribution.

y.title: The modified Newtonian dynamics—MOND and its implications for new physics
y.abstract: No more salient issue exists in contemporary astrophysics and cosmology than that of the elusive ‘dark matter’. For many years already Milgrom's paradigm of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) has provided an alternative way to interpret observations without appeal to invisible dark matter. MOND had been successful in elucidating economically the dynamics of disc galaxies of all scales, while doing less well for clusters of galaxies; in its original form it could not address gravitational lensing or cosmology. After reviewing some of the evidence in favour of MOND, I recollect the development of relativistic formulations for it to cope with the last deficiency. I comment on recent work by various groups in confronting TeVeS, a relativistic embodiment of MOND, with observational data on gravitational lensing and cosmology. Throughout I ask what sort of physics can be responsible for the efficacy of MOND, and conclude with an appraisal of what theoretical developments are still needed to reach a full description of the world involving no unobserved matter.

tag.main_claim: The author reviews MOND as a viable alternative to dark matter for explaining galaxy dynamics, with its relativistic formulation TeVeS extending the framework to gravitational lensing and cosmology, though further theoretical development is still needed for a complete dark-matter-free description.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's central thesis is that galaxy dynamics can be explained without dark matter (Q1) via modified dynamics at low accelerations (Q2), and it highlights MOND's success in economically elucidating disc galaxy dynamics including scaling relations (Q3). If any of these were false, the paper's argument for MOND as a viable alternative framework would collapse.
tag.evidence_quote: Milgrom's paradigm of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) has provided an alternative way to interpret observations without appeal to invisible dark matter. MOND had been successful in elucidating economically the dynamics of disc galaxies of all scales

judge.conjunction: While dark matter density profiles such as BMO and DARKexp provide the best fits to galaxy cluster lensing mass profiles [x], MOND and its relativistic extension TeVeS offer a viable dark-matter-free alternative for explaining galaxy dynamics [y].
judge.x_background_statement: The gravitational lensing mass of galaxy clusters is dominated by non-baryonic dark matter distributed in collisionless halos, consistent with most matter in the universe being dark matter.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics can be fully explained by baryonic matter alone through a modified force law, without requiring any non-baryonic dark matter.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 asserts that most matter in the universe is non-baryonic dark matter, which must be present and gravitationally relevant in structures including galaxies. Q1 asserts that galaxy dynamics are explained by baryons alone with no dark matter. If non-baryonic dark matter constitutes most of the universe's matter and clusters around galaxies (as ΛCDM requires), it cannot simultaneously be absent from galaxy-scale dynamics. Conversely, if no dark matter is needed for galaxy dynamics (Q1), the universal dark matter budget of P1 is undermined.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Both dark matter halos and modified gravity are valid descriptions of gravitational phenomena, each governing a different scale—dark matter dominates cluster-scale lensing while modified gravity governs galaxy-scale dynamics—so a complete cosmological model should incorporate both.
judge.notes: Paper x's entire analysis presupposes that cluster lensing mass is dark matter halo mass (P1/P4); it never tests a MOND-based lensing model. Paper y explicitly frames MOND as eliminating the need for dark matter (Q1), and even notes MOND 'does less well for clusters,' which a careless reader might interpret as evidence that the two frameworks are complementary by regime. However, P1 is a universal claim about the matter content of the universe, not a cluster-specific one, and Q1 denies dark matter's necessity in principle. The orphan conclusion—that both frameworks are valid in their respective domains—is rejected by both: ΛCDM attributes galaxy dynamics to dark matter (P2, P3), and MOND attributes cluster mass discrepancies to modified gravity rather than collisionless dark matter (Q4). A verifier should check whether any hybrid dark-matter-plus-MOND model (e.g., dark matter only in clusters) is seriously entertained in either paper; paper y's abstract suggests MOND proponents seek to explain clusters without dark matter via TeVeS, supporting the conflict.

y.title: A new formulation of the external field effect in MOND and numerical simulations of ultra-diffuse dwarf galaxies – application to NGC 1052-DF2 and NGC 1052-DF4
y.abstract: The ultra-diffuse dwarf galaxy NGC 1052-DF2 (DF2) has 10 (11) measured globular clusters (GCs) with a line-of-sight velocity dispersion of |$\sigma =7.8^{+5.2}_{-2.2}\,$| km s−1 (⁠|$\sigma =10.6^{+3.9}_{-2.3}\,$| km s−1). Our conventional statistical analysis of the original 10 GCs gives |$\sigma =8.0^{+4.3}_{-3.0}\,$| km s−1. The overall distribution of velocities agrees well with a Gaussian of this width. Due to the non-linear Poisson equation in MOND, a dwarf galaxy has weaker self-gravity when in close proximity to a massive host. This external field effect is investigated using a new analytic formulation and fully self-consistent live N-body models in MOND. Our formulation agrees well with that of Famaey and McGaugh. These new simulations confirm our analytic results and suggest that DF2 may be in a deep-freeze state unique to MOND. The correctly calculated MOND velocity dispersion agrees with our inferred dispersion and that of van Dokkum et al. if DF2 is within 150 kpc of NGC 1052 and both are 20 Mpc away. The GCs of DF2 are however significantly brighter and larger than normal GCs, a problem which disappears if DF2 is significantly closer to us. A distance of 10–13 Mpc makes DF2 a normal dwarf galaxy even more consistent with MOND and the 13 Mpc distance reported by Trujillo et al.. We discuss the similar dwarf DF4, finding good agreement with MOND. We also discuss possible massive galaxies near DF2 and DF4 along with their distances and peculiar velocities, noting that NGC 1052 may lie at a distance near 10 Mpc.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the velocity dispersions of ultra-diffuse dwarfs NGC 1052-DF2 and DF4 are consistent with MOND predictions when the external field effect from a nearby host galaxy is properly accounted for.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim requires Q1 because the entire analysis assumes galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone without dark matter, and the consistency of predicted velocity dispersions with observations is meaningful only if dark matter is absent. The claim requires Q2 because the external field effect—which suppresses self-gravity in dwarfs near a massive host—arises directly from the non-linear MOND Poisson equation and the breakdown of Newtonian dynamics below a0.
tag.evidence_quote: Due to the non-linear Poisson equation in MOND, a dwarf galaxy has weaker self-gravity when in close proximity to a massive host. This external field effect is investigated using a new analytic formulation and fully self-consistent live N-body models in MOND.

judge.conjunction: Studies have shown that satellite galaxies in ΛCDM simulations follow the radial acceleration relation with larger scatter and no host-field effect [x], while the velocity dispersions of ultra-diffuse dwarfs NGC 1052-DF2 and DF4 are consistent with MOND predictions when the external field effect from a nearby host is properly accounted for [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Most matter in the universe is non-baryonic dark matter, and galaxy dynamics including satellite RAR behavior arise from gravitational interactions within dark matter halos governed by Newtonian/GR dynamics.
judge.y_background_statement: Galaxy dynamics are explained by baryonic matter alone without dark matter, and the non-linear MOND force law produces an external field effect that weakens self-gravity in the vicinity of a massive host.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 posits that non-baryonic dark matter is the dominant mass component governing galaxy dynamics, while Q1 holds that baryonic matter alone suffices and no dark matter exists. These are mutually exclusive ontologies: either dark matter halos produce the observed dynamics or modified gravity does, but not both.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Both dark matter halos (producing the RAR with scatter in satellites) and MOND's external field effect (explaining dwarf velocity dispersions) are real and coexist as explanations for satellite/dwarf galaxy dynamics, implying that elements of both incompatible theories are simultaneously valid.
judge.notes: Both papers address the same physical regime—satellite/dwarf galaxy dynamics in the gravitational field of a host—and paper x explicitly contrasts ΛCDM's no-host-effect prediction with MOND's external field effect, while paper y confirms that MOND's external field effect explains DF2/DF4. A verifier should confirm that paper x's RAR scatter result is a genuine ΛCDM simulation prediction (not an observational finding compatible with both frameworks) and that paper y's velocity dispersion match is specifically a MOND-only prediction (no dark-matter counterpart is offered). The orphan conclusion is clear: asserting both findings as true implies both dark matter and modified gravity operate simultaneously, which neither ΛCDM nor MOND accepts.

x.title: Rotation curves of rotating Galactic Bose-Einstein condensate dark matter halos
x.abstract: We present the dynamics of rotating Bose condensate Galactic dark matter halos, made of an ultralight spinless boson. We restrict to the case of adding axisymmetric rigid rotation to initially spherically symmetric structures and show there are three regimes: (i) small angular momentum, which basically retains the drawbacks of spherically symmetric halos related to compactness and failure at explaining Galactic rotation curves; (ii) an intermediate range of values of angular momentum that allow the existence of long-lived structures with acceptable rotation curve profiles; and (iii) high angular momentum, in which the structure is dispersed away by rotation. We also present in detail the new code used to solve the Gross--Pitaevskii Poisson system of equations in three dimensions.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that rotating Bose-Einstein condensate dark matter halos exhibit three dynamical regimes depending on angular momentum, with an intermediate range producing acceptable galactic rotation curve profiles.

y.title: Refining the MOND Interpolating Function and TeVeS Lagrangian
y.abstract: The phenomena customarily described with dark matter or modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) have been argued by Bekenstein to be the consequences of a covariant scalar field, controlled by a free function [related to the MOND interpolating function ( g / a 0 )] in its Lagrangian density. In the context of this relativistic MOND theory (TeVeS), we examine critically the interpolating function in the transition zone between weak and strong gravity. Bekenstein's toy model produces a that varies too gradually, and it fits rotation curves less well than the standard MOND interpolating function ( x ) = x /(1 + x 2 ) 1/2 . However, the latter varies too sharply and implies an implausible external field effect. These constraints on opposite sides have not yet excluded TeVeS, but they have made the zone of acceptable interpolating functions narrower. An acceptable "toy" Lagrangian density function with simple analytical properties is singled out for future studies of TeVeS in galaxies. We also suggest how to extend the model to solar system dynamics and cosmology.

judge.conjunction: Recent studies have examined galactic rotation curves from multiple theoretical perspectives, with work on rotating Bose-Einstein condensate dark matter halos identifying three dynamical regimes depending on angular momentum [x], and refinements to MOND interpolating functions in TeVeS narrowing the acceptable range through rotation-curve fitting and external-field-effect constraints [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Galactic rotation curves are explained by dark matter halos, specifically Bose-Einstein condensate halos made of ultralight bosons, so non-baryonic dark matter exists and governs galaxy-scale dynamics.
judge.y_background_statement: Galactic rotation curves are explained by baryonic matter alone through modified gravity (MOND/TeVeS), without any non-baryonic dark matter.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P1 asserts that non-baryonic dark matter is the cause of galactic dynamics, while Q1 asserts that baryonic matter alone suffices and no dark matter is needed. If dark matter halos explain rotation curves, then MOND's modification of gravity to explain those same curves without dark matter is unnecessary and vice versa; the two explanations are mutually exclusive accounts of the same phenomenon.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Galactic rotation curves can be explained by either dark matter halos or modified gravity, suggesting both frameworks offer complementary valid descriptions of the same phenomenon.
judge.notes: Both papers address the same empirical phenomenon—galactic rotation curves—from fundamentally incompatible theoretical standpoints. Paper x's entire model presupposes dark matter halos (P1), while paper y's TeVeS/MOND framework explicitly removes dark matter (Q1). A literature review citing both as if they are complementary approaches obscures the fact that accepting one explanation precludes the other. The orphan conclusion that 'both are valid' is rejected by both frameworks: Lambda-CDM does not endorse MOND as a real description of gravity, and MOND does not endorse dark matter halos as real. No natural regime separation exists since both target the same galaxy-scale rotation-curve data.

x.title: Rotation curves of rotating Galactic Bose-Einstein condensate dark matter halos
x.abstract: We present the dynamics of rotating Bose condensate Galactic dark matter halos, made of an ultralight spinless boson. We restrict to the case of adding axisymmetric rigid rotation to initially spherically symmetric structures and show there are three regimes: (i) small angular momentum, which basically retains the drawbacks of spherically symmetric halos related to compactness and failure at explaining Galactic rotation curves; (ii) an intermediate range of values of angular momentum that allow the existence of long-lived structures with acceptable rotation curve profiles; and (iii) high angular momentum, in which the structure is dispersed away by rotation. We also present in detail the new code used to solve the Gross--Pitaevskii Poisson system of equations in three dimensions.

judge.x_background_statement: Newtonian gravity (the Poisson equation) correctly describes gravitational dynamics at galactic scales including very low accelerations, and galactic rotation curves are explained by the gravitational potential of dark matter halos.

If Newtonian dynamics hold at low accelerations, the MOND interpolating function that parameterizes the breakdown is physically meaningless; if they break down, BEC dark matter halo models computed with the Newtonian Poisson equation at galactic scales use incorrect dynamics.

x.title: Missing dark matter in dwarf galaxies?
x.abstract: We use cosmological hydrodynamical simulations of the APOSTLE project along with high-quality rotation curve observations to examine the fraction of baryons in ΛCDM haloes that collect into galaxies. This ‘galaxy formation efficiency’ correlates strongly and with little scatter with halo mass, dropping steadily towards dwarf galaxies. The baryonic mass of a galaxy may thus be used to place a lower limit on total halo mass and, consequently, on its asymptotic maximum circular velocity. A number of observed dwarfs seem to violate this constraint, having baryonic masses up to 10 times higher than expected from their rotation speeds, or, alternatively, rotating at only half the speed expected for their mass. Taking the data at face value, either these systems have formed galaxies with extraordinary efficiency – highly unlikely given their shallow potential wells – or their dark matter content is much lower than expected from ΛCDM haloes. This ‘missing dark matter’ is reminiscent of the inner mass deficit of galaxies with slowly rising rotation curves, but cannot be explained away by star formation-induced ‘cores’ in the dark mass profile, since the anomalous deficit applies to regions larger than the luminous galaxies themselves. We argue that explaining the structure of these galaxies would require either substantial modification of the standard ΛCDM paradigm or else significant revision to the uncertainties in their inferred mass profiles, which should be much larger than reported. Systematic errors in inclination may provide a simple resolution to what would otherwise be a rather intractable problem for the current paradigm.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that some observed dwarf galaxies appear to contain significantly less dark matter than predicted by their baryonic masses in the ΛCDM framework, posing a challenge that may require paradigm modification or revision of mass-profile uncertainties.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim requires that galaxies reside in non-baryonic dark matter haloes (P1) whose expected masses can be inferred from baryonic content, and that rotation speeds are interpreted via Newtonian dynamics to infer total masses (P2). If dark matter haloes did not exist or if dynamics were modified at low accelerations, the 'missing dark matter' discrepancy would not arise in the same way.
tag.evidence_quote: Taking the data at face value, either these systems have formed galaxies with extraordinary efficiency – highly unlikely given their shallow potential wells – or their dark matter content is much lower than expected from ΛCDM haloes.

y.title: Dynamical friction in modified Newtonian dynamics
y.abstract: We have tested a previous analytical estimate of the dynamical friction time-scale in modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) with fully non-linear N-body simulations. The simulations confirm that the dynamical friction time-scale is significantly shorter in MOND than in equivalent Newtonian systems, i.e. systems with the same phase-space distribution of baryons and additional dark matter. An apparent conflict between this result and the long time-scales determined for bars to slow and mergers to be completed in previous N-body simulations of MOND systems is explained. The confirmation of the short dynamical-friction time-scale in MOND underlines the challenge that the Fornax dwarf spheroidal poses to the viability of MOND.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that dynamical friction timescales are significantly shorter in MOND than in equivalent Newtonian dark-matter systems, posing a challenge to MOND's viability in explaining the Fornax dwarf spheroidal.
tag.dependence_explanation: The short dynamical-friction timescale is a direct consequence of MOND's modified force law at low accelerations (Q2). Without the breakdown of Newtonian dynamics below a0, there is no MOND-specific enhancement of dynamical friction to report.
tag.evidence_quote: The simulations confirm that the dynamical friction time-scale is significantly shorter in MOND than in equivalent Newtonian systems, i.e. systems with the same phase-space distribution of baryons and additional dark matter.

judge.conjunction: Recent studies have shown that some dwarf galaxies contain significantly less dark matter than predicted by ΛCDM [x], while dynamical friction timescales computed in MOND challenge its viability for systems like the Fornax dwarf spheroidal [y].
judge.x_background_statement: Newtonian dynamics remain valid at the low accelerations characteristic of dwarf galaxies, so rotation curve velocities directly indicate the total gravitating mass.
judge.y_background_statement: Newtonian dynamics break down below the characteristic acceleration a0, so the MOND force law governs dynamical processes such as dynamical friction in dwarf galaxies.
judge.why_backgrounds_conflict: P2 asserts Newtonian dynamics hold at very low accelerations—the regime of dwarf galaxies—while Q2 asserts they break down below a0; the same low-acceleration regime cannot simultaneously obey and violate Newtonian dynamics.
judge.orphan_conclusion: Neither ΛCDM nor MOND can adequately explain dwarf galaxy dynamics, necessitating a third theoretical framework.
judge.notes: Both papers operate in the low-acceleration regime of dwarf galaxies, so the P2 vs Q2 conflict cannot be resolved by regime scoping. A verifier should confirm that paper x's mass inferences from rotation curves genuinely require Newtonian dynamics at low accelerations, since the paper also invokes cosmological abundance matching which might be argued as separable from the dynamical mass inference. Paper y's dependence on Q2 is direct and unambiguous—the entire N-body simulation uses the MOND force law.

x.title: Breakdown of the Newton–Einstein Standard Gravity at Low Acceleration in Internal Dynamics of Wide Binary Stars
x.abstract: Abstract A gravitational anomaly is found at weak gravitational acceleration g N ≲ 10−9 m s−2 from analyses of the dynamics of wide binary stars selected from the Gaia DR3 database that have accurate distances, proper motions, and reliably inferred stellar masses. Implicit high-order multiplicities are required and the multiplicity fraction is calibrated so that binary internal motions agree statistically with Newtonian dynamics at a high enough acceleration of ≈10−8 m s−2. The observed sky-projected motions and separation are deprojected to the 3D relative velocity v and separation r through a Monte Carlo method, and a statistical relation between the Newtonian acceleration g N ≡ GM/r 2 (where M is the total mass of the binary system) and a kinematic acceleration g ≡ v 2/r is compared with the corresponding relation predicted by Newtonian dynamics. The empirical acceleration relation at ≲10−9 m s−2 systematically deviates from the Newtonian expectation. A gravitational anomaly parameter δ obs−newt between the observed acceleration at g N and the Newtonian prediction is measured to be: δ obs−newt = 0.034 ± 0.007 and 0.109 ± 0.013 at g N ≈ 10−8.91 and 10−10.15 m s−2, from the main sample of 26,615 wide binaries within 200 pc. These two deviations in the same direction represent a 10σ significance. The deviation represents a direct evidence for the breakdown of standard gravity at weak acceleration. At g N = 10−10.15 m s−2, the observed to Newton-predicted acceleration ratio is g obs / g pred = 10 2 δ obs − newt = 1.43 ± 0.06 . This systematic deviation agrees with the boost factor that the AQUAL theory predicts for kinematic accelerations in circular orbits under the Galactic external field.

tag.main_claim: Chae shows that wide binary stars exhibit a breakdown of Newtonian gravity at low accelerations (~10^-9 m/s^2), with observed accelerations exceeding Newtonian predictions by a factor consistent with AQUAL/MOND theory.
tag.dependence_explanation: The central claim that standard gravity breaks down at low accelerations directly requires Q2, which states that Newtonian dynamics fail below a characteristic acceleration a0. The paper's interpretation of the observed deviation as a fundamental gravity breakdown—and its agreement with AQUAL predictions—only makes sense if Newtonian dynamics are indeed modified at low accelerations.
tag.evidence_quote: The deviation represents a direct evidence for the breakdown of standard gravity at weak acceleration. At g N = 10 −10.15 m s−2, the observed to Newton-predicted acceleration ratio is g obs / g pred = 10 2 δ obs − newt = 1.43 ± 0.06 . This systematic deviation agrees with the boost factor that the AQUAL theory predicts for kinematic accelerations in circular orbits under the Galactic external field.

y.title: Measurements of the Low-acceleration Gravitational Anomaly from the Normalized Velocity Profile of Gaia Wide Binary Stars and Statistical Testing of Newtonian and Milgromian Theories
y.abstract: Abstract Low-acceleration gravitational anomaly is investigated with a new method of exploiting the normalized velocity profile v ˜ ≡ v p / v c of wide binary stars as a function of the normalized sky-projected radius s/r M, where v p is the sky-projected relative velocity between the pair, v c is the Newtonian circular velocity at the sky-projected separation s, and r M is the MOND radius. With a Monte Carlo method, Gaia observed binaries and their virtual Newtonian counterparts are probabilistically distributed on the s/r M versus v ˜ plane, and a logarithmic velocity ratio parameter Γ is measured in the bins of s/r M. With three samples of binaries covering a broad range in size, data quality, and implied fraction of hierarchical systems including a new sample of 6389 binaries selected with accurate distances and radial velocities, I find a unanimous systematic variation from the Newtonian flat line. With Γ = 0 at s/r M ≲ 0.15 or s ≲ 1 kau, I get Γ = 0.068 ± 0.015 (stat) − 0.015 + 0.024 (syst) for s/r M ≳ 0.7 or s ≳ 5 kau. The gravitational anomaly (i.e., acceleration boost) factor given by γ g = 102Γ is measured to be γ g = 1.37 − 0.09 + 0.10 (stat) − 0.09 + 0.16 (syst). With a reduced χ 2 test of Newtonian and Milgromian nonrelativistic theories, I find that Newtonian gravity is ruled out at 5.8σ ( χ ν 2 = 9.4 ) by the new sample (and 9.2σ by the largest sample used). The Milgromian AQUAL theory is acceptable with 0.7 ≲ χ ν 2 ≲ 3.1 . These results agree well with earlier results with the “acceleration-plane analysis” for a variety of samples and the “stacked velocity profile analysis” for a pure binary sample.

tag.main_claim: Chae (2024) shows that wide binary stars exhibit a gravitational anomaly at low accelerations consistent with Milgromian (MOND/AQUAL) dynamics and inconsistent with Newtonian gravity, ruling out Newtonian gravity at 5.8σ.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's central claim that Newtonian gravity is ruled out in favor of Milgromian dynamics directly depends on Q2, which posits that Newtonian dynamics break down below a characteristic acceleration a0. The entire analysis is structured around testing dynamics near the MOND radius and acceleration scale, and the claimed anomaly only makes sense if Q2 is true.
tag.evidence_quote: With a reduced χ 2 test of Newtonian and Milgromian nonrelativistic theories, I find that Newtonian gravity is ruled out at 5.8σ ( χ ν 2 = 9.4 ) by the new sample (and 9.2σ by the largest sample used). The Milgromian AQUAL theory is acceptable with 0.7 ≲ χ ν 2 ≲ 3.1 .

judge.conjunction: Analyses of Gaia wide binary stars have revealed a consistent gravitational anomaly at low accelerations, with observed accelerations exceeding Newtonian predictions by a factor of roughly 1.4 in a manner compatible with AQUAL/MOND expectations, thereby challenging the validity of Newtonian gravity in the low-acceleration regime [x,y].
judge.notes: Both papers are by the same author (Chae) and draw on overlapping Gaia DR3 datasets with similar methodologies, so they do not constitute fully independent confirmations. The reported boost factors differ slightly (1.43 ± 0.06 vs. 1.37 with larger systematic errors), and paper y notes AQUAL is only marginally acceptable (0.7 ≲ χ²ν ≲ 3.1), meaning MOND is not definitively favored over Newtonian gravity in an absolute sense. Both studies must contend with the systematic uncertainty of unresolved hierarchical multiples contaminating the binary samples, which remains the dominant alternative explanation. Additionally, both papers operate within Framework Q (MOND); if a reviewer requires consistency with Framework P (ΛCDM), these claims directly conflict with P2 (Newtonian dynamics hold at low accelerations), making the conjunction problematic in that broader theoretical context.

x.title: High-Resolution Rotation Curves of Low Surface Brightness Galaxies. II. Mass Models
x.abstract: We present mass models for a sample of 30 high-resolution rotation curves of low surface brightness galaxies. We fit both pseudoisothermal (core dominated) and cold dark matter (CDM; cusp dominated) halos for a wide variety of assumptions about the stellar mass-to-light ratio. We find that the pseudoisothermal model provides superior fits. CDM fits show systematic deviations from the data and often have a small statistical likelihood of being the appropriate model. The distribution of concentration parameters is too broad, and has too low a mean, to be explained by low-density, flat CDM (ΛCDM). This failing becomes more severe as increasing allowance is made for stellar mass: Navarro, Frenk, & White (NFW) model fits require uncomfortably low mass-to-light ratios. In contrast, the maximum disk procedure does often succeed in predicting the inner shape of the rotation curves, but it requires uncomfortably large stellar mass-to-light ratios. The data do admit reasonable stellar population mass-to-light ratios if halos have cores rather than cusps.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that pseudoisothermal (core-dominated) dark matter halos provide superior fits to rotation curves of low surface brightness galaxies compared to cuspy CDM (NFW) halos, and that the distribution of concentration parameters is inconsistent with ΛCDM predictions.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis assumes galaxies are surrounded by dark matter halos (P1) and uses Newtonian dynamics to infer mass distributions from rotation curves (P2). If dark matter does not exist or if Newtonian dynamics break down at low accelerations, the mass models and their fitted halo profiles would be meaningless.
tag.evidence_quote: We fit both pseudoisothermal (core dominated) and cold dark matter (CDM; cusp dominated) halos for a wide variety of assumptions about the stellar mass-to-light ratio.

y.title: High‐Resolution Optical Velocity Fields of 11 Low Surface Brightness Galaxies
y.abstract: We present high-resolution two-dimensional velocity fields from integral field spectroscopy, along with derived rotation curves for 11 low surface brightness galaxies.
