We fit NFW and pseudoisothermal halo models to the new data combined with previous long-slit and H I data. In most cases, we find the pseudoisothermal halo to better represent the data than the NFW halo, as the NFW concentrations are often lower than expected for a ΛCDM cosmology. We also compare our results to previous studies and find that including the new two-dimensional optical data does not significantly alter the halo parameters but does decrease the uncertainties by roughly a factor of 2.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that pseudoisothermal dark matter halos better represent the rotation curves of low surface brightness galaxies than NFW halos, with NFW concentrations often lower than expected for ΛCDM cosmology.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis consists of fitting dark matter halo models (NFW and pseudoisothermal) to rotation curves, which requires that galaxies are dominated by non-baryonic dark matter (P1) and that Newtonian dynamics hold at low accelerations so that observed velocities can be interpreted via standard mass profiles (P2).
tag.evidence_quote: We fit NFW and pseudoisothermal halo models to the new data combined with previous long-slit and H I data. In most cases, we find the pseudoisothermal halo to better represent the data than the NFW halo, as the NFW concentrations are often lower than expected for a ΛCDM cosmology.

judge.conjunction: Analyses of low surface brightness galaxy rotation curves have repeatedly found that core-dominated pseudoisothermal dark matter halos provide superior fits compared to cuspy NFW halos, and that the resulting NFW concentration parameters fall below the values expected in a ΛCDM cosmology [x, y].
judge.notes: Both papers operate within Framework P (ΛCDM), so there is no cross-framework conflict. The two claims are nearly identical rather than complementary, so the conjunction is unproblematic; however, the reviewer should note that paper y's sample of 11 galaxies partly overlaps with and explicitly builds upon earlier long-slit studies such as paper x's 30-galaxy sample, meaning the two results are not fully independent lines of evidence. Paper y's main contribution is confirming with 2D integral-field data that the earlier long-slit-based conclusions hold, rather than providing a genuinely separate test.

x.title: Rotation Curves of Ursa Major Galaxies in the Context of Modified Newtonian Dynamics
x.abstract: This is the third in a series of papers in which spiral galaxy rotation curves are considered in the context of Milgrom's modified dynamics (MOND). The present sample of 30 objects is drawn from a complete sample of galaxies in the Ursa Major cluster, with photometric data from Tully et al. and 21 cm line data from Verheijen. The galaxies are roughly all at the same distance (15 to 16 Mpc). The radio observations are made with the Westerbork Synthesis Array, which means that the linear resolution of all rotation curves is comparable. The greatest advantage of this sample is the existence of K '-band surface photometry for all galaxies; the near-infrared emission, being relatively free of the effects of dust absorption and less sensitive to recent star formation, is a more precise tracer of the mean radial distribution of the dominant stellar population. The predicted rotation curves are calculated from the K '-band surface photometry and the observed distribution of neutral hydrogen using the simple MOND prescription, in which the one adjustable parameter is the mass of the stellar disk or the implied mass-to-light ratio. The predicted rotation curves generally agree with the observed curves, and the mean M / L in the near-infrared is about 0.9 with a small dispersion. The fitted M / L in the B -band correlates with B - V color in the sense predicted by population synthesis models. Including earlier work, about 80 galaxy rotation curves are now well reproduced from the observed distribution of detectable matter using the MOND formula to calculate the gravitational acceleration; this lends considerable observational support to Milgrom's unconventional hypothesis.

tag.main_claim: Sanders shows that MOND reproduces the rotation curves of about 80 galaxies from the observed distribution of baryonic matter alone, with mass-to-light ratios consistent with stellar population synthesis predictions.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's central claim requires that galaxy dynamics can be explained by baryonic matter without dark matter (Q1) and that Newtonian dynamics break down at low accelerations, necessitating the MOND formula to calculate gravitational acceleration (Q2). The rotation curves are predicted using only the observed distribution of stars and gas via the MOND prescription.
tag.evidence_quote: The predicted rotation curves are calculated from the K '-band surface photometry and the observed distribution of neutral hydrogen using the simple MOND prescription, in which the one adjustable parameter is the mass of the stellar disk or the implied mass-to-light ratio. The predicted rotation curves generally agree with the observed curves... about 80 galaxy rotation curves are now well reproduced from the observed distribution of detectable matter using the MOND formula to calculate the gravitational acceleration

y.title: THINGS about MOND
y.abstract: We present an analysis of 12 high-resolution galactic rotation curves from The HI Nearby Galaxy Survey (THINGS) in the context of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND). These rotation curves were selected to be the most reliable for mass modelling, and they are the highest quality rotation curves currently available for a sample of galaxies spanning a wide range of luminosities. We fit the rotation curves with the “simple” and “standard” interpolating functions of MOND, and we find that the “simple” function yields better results. We also redetermine the value of a0, and find a median value very close to the one determined in previous studies, a0 = (1.22 ± 0.33) × 10-8 cm s-2. Leaving the distance as a free parameter within the uncertainty of its best independently determined value leads to excellent quality fits for 75% of the sample. Among the three exceptions, two are also known to give relatively poor fits in Newtonian dynamics plus dark matter. The remaining case (NGC 3198) presents some tension between the observations and the MOND fit, which might, however, be explained by the presence of non-circular motions, by a small distance, or by a value of a0 at the lower end of our best-fit interval, 0.9 × 10-8 cm s-2. The best-fit stellar M/L ratios are generally in remarkable agreement with the predictions of stellar population synthesis models. We also show that the narrow range of gravitational accelerations found to be generated by dark matter in galaxies is consistent with the narrow range of additional gravity predicted by MOND.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that MOND with the 'simple' interpolating function successfully fits high-quality THINGS rotation curves, yielding a consistent value of a0 and stellar mass-to-light ratios in agreement with population synthesis models.
tag.dependence_explanation: The analysis fits rotation curves using only baryonic matter (stars and gas) with MOND interpolating functions and the acceleration constant a0, requiring both that Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2) and that baryonic matter alone explains galaxy rotation without dark matter (Q1).
tag.evidence_quote: We fit the rotation curves with the “simple” and “standard” interpolating functions of MOND, and we find that the “simple” function yields better results. We also redetermine the value of a0, and find a median value very close to the one determined in previous studies, a0 = (1.22 ± 0.33) × 10-8 cm s-2.

judge.conjunction: Studies of galaxy rotation curves have consistently shown that MOND reproduces observed kinematics from the baryonic mass distribution alone with mass-to-light ratios consistent with stellar population synthesis predictions, from Sanders's sample of approximately 80 Ursa Major galaxies [x] to the high-resolution THINGS survey confirming the 'simple' interpolating function and a consistent value of a0 [y].
judge.notes: Both papers operate within Framework Q (MOND), so their claims share a consistent theoretical background and the conjunction is largely unproblematic. The two studies differ in sample size and data quality: Sanders (1998) uses ~80 galaxies with moderate-resolution 21 cm data, while the THINGS paper (2010) examines 12 high-resolution rotation curves. The THINGS analysis finds that 25% of its sample (3/12, including NGC 3198) shows some tension with MOND fits, slightly qualifying the combined claim. Both papers converge on the 'simple' interpolating function and consistent M/L ratios, reinforcing rather than contradicting each other.

x.title: Galaxy Formation: Cold Dark Matter, Feedback, and the Hubble Sequence
x.abstract: TreeSPH simulations of galaxy formation in a standard Λ cold dark matter cosmology, including star formation and the effects of energetic stellar feedback processes and of a metagalactic UV field, have been performed, resulting in a mix of realistic disk, lenticular, and elliptical galaxies at redshift z = 0. The disk galaxies are deficient in angular momentum by only about a factor of 2 compared with observed disk galaxies for simulations with fairly strong starbursts in early, protogalactic clouds, leading to "blow-away" of the remaining gas in the clouds. In this respect the present scenario is hence doing almost as well as the warm dark matter (WDM) scenarios discussed by Sommer-Larsen & Dolgov. The surface density profiles of the stellar disks are approximately exponential, and those of the bulges range from exponential to r 1/4 , as observed. The bulge-to-disk ratios of the disk galaxies are consistent with observations, as are their integrated B - V colors, which have been calculated using stellar population synthesis techniques. Furthermore, the observed I -band Tully-Fisher relation can be matched, provided that the stellar mass-to-light ratio of disk galaxies is M / L I ~ 0.8, similar to what was found by Sommer-Larsen & Dolgov from their WDM simulations and in fair agreement with several recent observational determinations of M / L I for disk galaxies. The elliptical and lenticular galaxies have approximately r 1/4 stellar surface density profiles, are dominated by nondisklike kinematics, and are flattened as a result of nonisotropic stellar velocity distributions, again consistent with observations. Hot halo gas is predicted to cool out and be accreted onto the Galactic disk at a rate of 0.5-1 M ☉ yr -1 at z = 0, consistent with upper limits deduced from Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer observations of O VI. We have analyzed in detail the formation history of two disk galaxies with circular speeds comparable to that of the Milky Way and find gas accretion rates, and hence bolometric X-ray luminosities of the halos, 6-7 times larger at z ~ 1 than at z = 0 for these disk galaxies. More generally, it is found that gas infall rates onto these disks are nearly exponentially declining with time, both for the total disk and for the "solar cylinder." This theoretical result hence supports the exponentially declining gas infall approximation often used in chemical evolution models. The infall timescales deduced are ~5-6 Gyr, comparable to what is adopted in current chemical evolution models to solve the "G dwarf problem." The disk of one of the two galaxies forms "inside-out," the other "outside-in," but in both cases the mean ages of the stars in the outskirts of the disks are ≳6-8 Gyr, fairly consistent with the findings of Ferguson & Johnson for the disk of M31. The amount of hot gas in disk galaxy halos is consistent with observational upper limits. The globular cluster M53 and the LMC are "inserted" in the halos of the two Milky Way-like disk galaxies, and dispersion measures to these objects are calculated. The results are consistent with upper limits from observed dispersion measures to pulsars in these systems. Finally, the results of the simulations indicate that the observed peak in the cosmic star formation rate at redshift z ~ 2 can be reproduced. Depending on the star formation and feedback scenarios, one predicts either a cosmic star formation rate that decreases monotonically with redshift beyond these redshifts or a second peak at z ~ 6-8, corresponding to the putative Population III and interestingly similar to recent estimates of the redshift at which the universe was reionized. These various scenarios should hence be observationally constrainable with upcoming instruments such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter Array.

tag.main_claim: Sommer-Larsen et al. show that ΛCDM galaxy formation simulations including stellar feedback can reproduce the Hubble sequence of galaxies, the observed Tully-Fisher relation, and other galaxy properties.
tag.dependence_explanation: The simulations are performed within a standard ΛCDM cosmology that assumes non-baryonic dark matter dominates the matter budget (P1), use standard Newtonian gravity in the TreeSPH code (P2), and reproduce the Tully-Fisher relation through galaxy formation and feedback processes rather than as a fundamental law (P3).
tag.evidence_quote: TreeSPH simulations of galaxy formation in a standard Λ cold dark matter cosmology, including star formation and the effects of energetic stellar feedback processes and of a metagalactic UV field, have been performed, resulting in a mix of realistic disk, lenticular, and elliptical galaxies at redshift z = 0. Furthermore, the observed I -band Tully-Fisher relation can be matched, provided that the stellar mass-to-light ratio of disk galaxies is M / L I ~ 0.8

y.title: Disk Galaxy Formation in a Λ Cold Dark Matter Universe
y.abstract: We describe hydrodynamic simulations of galaxy formation in a Λ cold dark matter cosmology, performed using a subresolution model for star formation and feedback in a multiphase interstellar medium (ISM). In particular, we demonstrate the formation of a well-resolved disk galaxy. The surface brightness profile of the galaxy is exponential, with a B -band central surface brightness of 21.0 mag arcsec -2 and a scale length of R d = 2.0 h -1 kpc. We find no evidence for a significant bulge component. The simulated galaxy falls within the I -band Tully-Fisher relation, with an absolute magnitude of I = -21.2 and a peak stellar rotation velocity of V rot = 121.3 km s -1 . While the total specific angular momentum of the stars in the galaxy agrees with observations, the angular momentum in the inner regions appears to be low by a factor of ~2. The star formation rate of the galaxy peaks at ~7 M ☉ yr -1 between redshifts z = 2 and 4, with the mean stellar age decreasing from ~10 Gyr in the outer regions of the disk to ~7.5 Gyr in the center, indicating that the disk did not simply form inside-out. The stars exhibit a metallicity gradient from 0.7 Z ☉ at the edge of the disk to 1.3 Z ☉ in the center. Using a suite of idealized galaxy formation simulations with different models for the ISM, we show that the effective pressure support provided by star formation and feedback in our multiphase model is instrumental in allowing the formation of large, stable disk galaxies. If ISM gas is instead modeled with an isothermal equation of state, or if star formation is suppressed entirely, growing gaseous disks quickly violate the Toomre stability criterion and undergo catastrophic fragmentation.

tag.main_claim: Abadi et al. show that hydrodynamic simulations in a ΛCDM cosmology with a multiphase ISM model and star formation feedback can produce realistic disk galaxies matching observed properties including the Tully-Fisher relation.
tag.dependence_explanation: The simulations are explicitly performed within a ΛCDM cosmology, requiring that dark matter exists (P1) and that Newtonian dynamics govern the gravitational physics (P2). The paper's use of the Tully-Fisher relation as a benchmark for the simulation's success presumes that this relation emerges from galaxy formation processes rather than being a fundamental law (P3); if Q3 held instead, reproducing the relation in a CDM simulation would not validate the formation model.
tag.evidence_quote: We describe hydrodynamic simulations of galaxy formation in a Λ cold dark matter cosmology, performed using a subresolution model for star formation and feedback in a multiphase interstellar medium (ISM). ... The simulated galaxy falls within the I -band Tully-Fisher relation, with an absolute magnitude of I = -21.2 and a peak stellar rotation velocity of V rot = 121.3 km s -1 .

judge.conjunction: ΛCDM hydrodynamic simulations incorporating stellar feedback have been shown to produce realistic disk galaxies satisfying the observed Tully-Fisher relation and other galaxy properties, including the formation of exponential stellar disks and the broader Hubble sequence (Sommer-Larsen et al. 2003; Abadi et al. 2004).
judge.notes: Both papers sit squarely within Framework P, so no deep theoretical conflict arises. However, the conjunction glosses over some differences: Sommer-Larsen et al. report a mix of disk, lenticular, and elliptical galaxies (the full Hubble sequence), whereas Abadi et al. focus on a single well-resolved disk galaxy with no significant bulge component. Both papers note an angular momentum deficit of roughly a factor of two, which could be seen as a shared limitation rather than a contradiction. Additionally, Sommer-Larsen et al. reproduce the Tully-Fisher relation contingent on a specific stellar mass-to-light ratio (M/L_I ~ 0.8), while Abadi et al. obtain a single galaxy lying on the relation; the scope of the Tully-Fisher 'match' thus differs between the two studies.

x.title: Galactic cannibalism and cold dark matter density profiles
x.abstract: Using N-body simulations, we show that the process of formation of the brightest cluster galaxy through dissipationless galactic cannibalism can affect the inner cluster dark matter density profile. In particular, we use as a realistic test case the dynamical evolution of the galaxy cluster C0337−2522 at redshift z= 0.59, hosting in its centre a group of five elliptical galaxies which are likely to be the progenitor of a central giant elliptical. After the formation of the brightest cluster galaxy, the inner cluster dark matter density profile is significantly flatter (logarithmic slope 0.49 ≲β≲ 0.90) than the original cusp (β= 1), as a consequence of dynamical friction heating of the massive galaxies against the diffuse cluster dark matter. In our simulations we have assumed that the cluster galaxies are made of stars only. We also show that the presence of galactic dark matter haloes can steepen the cluster central density profile. We conclude that galactic cannibalism could be a viable physical mechanism to reconcile – at least at the cluster scale – the flat dark matter haloes inferred observationally in some galaxy clusters with the steep haloes predicted by cosmological simulations.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that galactic cannibalism during brightest cluster galaxy formation can flatten the inner cluster dark matter density profile via dynamical friction heating, potentially reconciling observed flat-core clusters with cuspy profiles predicted by CDM simulations.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire simulation assumes the cluster is filled with collisionless dark matter (P1, P4) and evolves under Newtonian dynamics (P2). If dark matter did not exist or clusters were not dark-matter-dominated, the mechanism of dynamical friction against diffuse cluster dark matter would be meaningless, and the claim about reconciling density profiles would collapse.
tag.evidence_quote: the inner cluster dark matter density profile is significantly flatter (logarithmic slope 0.49 ≲β≲ 0.90) than the original cusp (β= 1), as a consequence of dynamical friction heating of the massive galaxies against the diffuse cluster dark matter.

y.title: THE CUSP/CORE PROBLEM AND THE SECONDARY INFALL MODEL
y.abstract: We study the cusp/core problem using a secondary infall model that takes into account the effect of ordered and random angular momentum, dynamical friction, and baryons adiabatic contraction (AC). The model is applied to structures on galactic scales (normal and dwarfs spiral galaxies) and on clusters of galaxies scales. Our analysis suggest that angular momentum and dynamical friction are able, on galactic scales, to overcome the competing effect of AC eliminating the cusp. The slope of density profile of inner halos flattens with decreasing halo mass and the profile is well approximated by a Burkert's profile. In order to obtain the Navarro–Frenk–White (NFW) profile, starting from the profiles obtained from our model, the magnitude of angular momentum and dynamical friction must be reduced with respect to the values predicted by the model itself. The rotation curves of four lower sideband galaxies from Gentile et al. are compared to the rotation curves obtained by the model in the present paper obtaining a good fit to the observational data. The time evolution of the density profile of a galaxy of 10 8 –10 9 M ☉ shows that after a transient steepening, due to the AC, the density profile flattens to α ≃ 0. On cluster scales we observe a similar evolution of the dark matter (DM) density profile but in this case the density profile slope flattens to α ≃ 0.6 for a cluster of ≃10 14 M ☉ . The total mass profile, differently from that of DM, shows a central cusp well fitted by an NFW model.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that angular momentum and dynamical friction can overcome adiabatic contraction to flatten dark matter halo cusps into core-like profiles on galactic scales, while on cluster scales the dark matter profile flattens to a lesser degree.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis assumes dark matter halos exist and dominate galactic and cluster mass (P1, P4), and uses standard Newtonian dynamical processes—dynamical friction, angular momentum, adiabatic contraction—to explain density profile evolution (P2). Without dark matter halos there is no cusp/core problem to solve, and the mechanisms invoked are standard-dynamics phenomena.
tag.evidence_quote: Our analysis suggest that angular momentum and dynamical friction are able, on galactic scales, to overcome the competing effect of AC eliminating the cusp. The slope of density profile of inner halos flattens with decreasing halo mass and the profile is well approximated by a Burkert's profile.

judge.conjunction: Within the CDM framework, dynamical friction-driven processes have been proposed to reconcile cuspy predicted dark matter profiles with observed cores: galactic cannibalism during brightest cluster galaxy formation flattens the inner cluster dark matter density profile via dynamical friction heating [x], and similarly, angular momentum combined with dynamical friction can overcome adiabatic contraction to flatten dark matter cusps on both galactic and cluster scales [y].
judge.notes: The conjunction is largely unproblematic since both papers operate within Framework P (Lambda-CDM) and both invoke dynamical friction as a core mechanism. However, a few nuances should be flagged: (1) Paper x isolates galactic cannibalism as the driver and assumes cluster galaxies are made of stars only, while Paper y includes baryonic adiabatic contraction as a competing effect that must be overcome—these are not contradictory but represent different modeling choices that could interact in ways neither paper fully addresses. (2) Paper y notes that recovering NFW profiles requires reducing angular momentum and dynamical friction below model-predicted values, suggesting their model may overestimate flattening, which could modestly tension with Paper x's claim that such mechanisms reconcile observations. (3) Paper y distinguishes between the dark matter mass profile (which flattens) and the total mass profile (which retains a cusp), a subtlety absent from Paper x's analysis.

x.title: ΛCDM is Consistent with SPARC Radial Acceleration Relation
x.abstract: Abstract Recent analysis of the Spitzer Photometry and Accurate Rotation Curve (SPARC) galaxy sample found a surprisingly tight relation between the radial acceleration inferred from the rotation curves and the acceleration due to the baryonic components of the disk. It has been suggested that this relation may be evidence for new physics, beyond ΛCDM. In this Letter, we show that 32 galaxies from the MUGS2 match the SPARC acceleration relation. These cosmological simulations of star-forming, rotationally supported disks were simulated with a WMAP3 ΛCDM cosmology, and match the SPARC acceleration relation with less scatter than the observational data. These results show that this acceleration relation is a consequence of dissipative collapse of baryons, rather than being evidence for exotic dark-sector physics or new dynamical laws.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the SPARC radial acceleration relation arises naturally from dissipative collapse of baryons in ΛCDM simulations, rather than requiring modified dynamics or new fundamental laws.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim relies on P1 because the simulations are ΛCDM cosmological simulations with dark matter halos; without dark matter the simulation setup is invalid. It relies on P2 because the simulations use Newtonian gravity, so if dynamics break down at low accelerations the simulated relation would be meaningless. It directly asserts P3, that the radial acceleration relation emerges from galaxy formation physics rather than being a fundamental law.
tag.evidence_quote: These cosmological simulations of star-forming, rotationally supported disks were simulated with a WMAP3 ΛCDM cosmology, and match the SPARC acceleration relation with less scatter than the observational data. These results show that this acceleration relation is a consequence of dissipative collapse of baryons, rather than being evidence for exotic dark-sector physics or new dynamical laws.

y.title: The radial acceleration relation in a ΛCDM universe
y.abstract: ABSTRACT We study the radial acceleration relation (RAR) between the total (atot) and baryonic (abary) centripetal acceleration profiles of central galaxies in the cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm. We analytically show that the RAR is intimately connected with the physics of the quasi-adiabatic relaxation of dark matter in the presence of baryons in deep potential wells. This cleanly demonstrates how the mean RAR and its scatter emerge in the low-acceleration regime ($10^{-12}{\rm \, m\, s}^{-2}\lesssim a_{\rm bary}\lesssim 10^{-10}{\rm \, m\, s}^{-2}$) from an interplay between baryonic feedback processes and the distribution of CDM in dark haloes. Our framework allows us to go further and study both higher and lower accelerations in detail, using analytical approximations and a realistic mock catalogue of ${\sim}342\, 000$ low-redshift central galaxies with Mr ≤ −19. We show that, while the RAR in the baryon-dominated high-acceleration regime ($a_{\rm bary}\gtrsim 10^{-10}{\rm \, m\, s}^{-2}$) is very sensitive to details of the relaxation physics, a simple ‘baryonification’ prescription matching the relaxation results of hydrodynamical CDM simulations is remarkably successful in reproducing the observed RAR without any tuning. And in the (currently unobserved) ultra-low-acceleration regime ($a_{\rm bary}\lesssim 10^{-12}{\rm \, m\, s}^{-2}$), the RAR is sensitive to the abundance of diffuse gas in the halo outskirts, with our default model predicting a distinctive break from a simple power-law-like relation for H i-deficient, diffuse gas-rich centrals. Our mocks also show that the RAR provides more robust, testable predictions of the ΛCDM paradigm at galactic scales, with implications for alternative gravity theories than the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that the radial acceleration relation emerges naturally in a ΛCDM universe from the quasi-adiabatic relaxation of dark matter in the presence of baryons, combined with baryonic feedback processes, without requiring modified gravity.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim requires that galaxies are dominated by non-baryonic dark matter (P1), since the entire mechanism involves CDM halo relaxation. It assumes Newtonian dynamics hold at low accelerations (P2), as the acceleration profiles are interpreted through standard dynamics. It also embodies P3: the RAR is a consequence of galaxy formation and feedback physics rather than a fundamental law of gravity.
tag.evidence_quote: We analytically show that the RAR is intimately connected with the physics of the quasi-adiabatic relaxation of dark matter in the presence of baryons in deep potential wells. This cleanly demonstrates how the mean RAR and its scatter emerge in the low-acceleration regime … from an interplay between baryonic feedback processes and the distribution of CDM in dark haloes.

judge.conjunction: The radial acceleration relation has been shown to arise naturally within ΛCDM, whether through the dissipative collapse of baryons in cosmological simulations [x] or through the quasi-adiabatic relaxation of dark matter in the presence of baryons combined with feedback processes [y], without requiring modified dynamics or new fundamental laws.
judge.notes: Both papers operate within Framework P and agree on the broad conclusion (RAR is consistent with ΛCDM, no need for MOND), but they emphasize different primary mechanisms: [x] stresses dissipative baryonic collapse as the driver, while [y] stresses dark matter quasi-adiabatic relaxation physics. These are not necessarily contradictory—they could be complementary descriptions at different levels—but the conjunction could mislead a reader into thinking the two studies identify the same causal mechanism, when in fact the relative roles assigned to baryonic dissipation versus dark halo relaxation differ. Additionally, [x] uses a small sample of 32 galaxies from MUGS2 simulations, while [y] uses analytical approximations and a mock catalogue of ~342,000 galaxies, so the methodological bases are quite different.

x.title: Dark matter density profiles in dwarf galaxies: linking Jeans modelling systematics and observation
x.abstract: ABSTRACT The distribution of dark matter in dwarf galaxies can have important implications on our understanding of galaxy formation as well as the particle physics properties of dark matter. However, accurately characterizing the dark matter content of dwarf galaxies is challenging due to limited data and complex dynamics that are difficult to accurately model. In this paper, we apply spherical Jeans modelling to simulated stellar kinematic data of spherical, isotropic dwarf galaxies with the goal of identifying the future observational directions that can improve the accuracy of the inferred dark matter distributions in the Milky Way dwarf galaxies. We explore how the dark matter inference is affected by the location and number of observed stars as well as the line-of-sight velocity measurement errors. We use mock observation to demonstrate the difficulty in constraining the inner core/cusp of the dark matter distribution with data sets of fewer than 10 000 stars. We also demonstrate the need for additional measurements to make robust estimates of the expected dark matter annihilation signal strength. For the purpose of deriving robust indirect detection constraints, we identify Ursa Major II, Ursa Minor, and Draco as the systems that would most benefit from additional stars being observed.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that constraining the inner core/cusp of dark matter distributions in Milky Way dwarf galaxies requires datasets of more than 10,000 stars, and identifies Ursa Major II, Ursa Minor, and Draco as the systems most benefiting from additional stellar observations for robust dark matter annihilation constraints.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis presumes that dwarf galaxies are dominated by non-baryonic dark matter whose density profile can be inferred (P1), and uses spherical Jeans modelling, which relies on Newtonian dynamics to relate stellar kinematics to the gravitational potential (P2).
tag.evidence_quote: The distribution of dark matter in dwarf galaxies can have important implications on our understanding of galaxy formation as well as the particle physics properties of dark matter.

y.title: Precise constraints on the dark matter content of Milky Way dwarf galaxies for gamma-ray experiments
y.abstract: We examine the prospects for detecting $\ensuremath{\gamma}$-rays from dark matter annihilation in the six most promising dwarf spheroidal (dSph) satellite galaxies of the Milky Way. We use recently measured velocity dispersion profiles to provide a systematic investigation of the dark matter mass distribution of each galaxy, and show that the uncertainty in the $\ensuremath{\gamma}$-ray flux from mass modeling is less than a factor of $\ensuremath{\sim}5$ for each dSph if we assume a smooth Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) profile. We show that Ursa Minor and Draco are the most promising dSphs for $\ensuremath{\gamma}$-ray detection with GLAST and other planned observatories. For each dSph, we investigate the flux enhancement resulting from halo substructure, and show that the enhancement factor relative to a smooth halo flux cannot be greater than about 100. This enhancement depends very weakly on the lower mass cutoff scale of the substructure mass function. While the amplitude of the expected flux from each dSph depends sensitively on the dark matter model, we show that the flux ratios between the six Sphs are known to within a factor of about 10. The flux ratios are also relatively insensitive to the current theoretical range of cold dark matter halo central slopes and substructure fractions.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that Ursa Minor and Draco are the most promising Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies for detecting gamma-rays from dark matter annihilation, and that flux ratios between the six best candidate dSphs are constrained to within a factor of ~10.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis presupposes that non-baryonic dark matter exists and forms halos around dwarf spheroidal galaxies, since the predicted gamma-ray signal arises from dark matter self-annihilation. If P1 were rejected, there would be no dark matter annihilation signal to predict or optimize targets for.
tag.evidence_quote: We examine the prospects for detecting $\gamma$-rays from dark matter annihilation in the six most promising dwarf spheroidal (dSph) satellite galaxies of the Milky Way. We use recently measured velocity dispersion profiles to provide a systematic investigation of the dark matter mass distribution of each galaxy

judge.conjunction: Ursa Minor and Draco have been identified as among the most promising Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies for detecting gamma-rays from dark matter annihilation, with flux ratios among candidate dSphs constrained to within a factor of ~10 [y], and subsequent work has shown that robustly constraining the inner core-versus-cusp structure of dark matter density profiles in these systems requires datasets exceeding 10,000 stars, highlighting Ursa Major II, Ursa Minor, and Draco as the systems most in need of additional stellar observations [x].
judge.notes: Both papers operate within Framework P (Lambda-CDM), so no foundational conflict arises. Minor tension: Paper y (2007) assumes a smooth NFW (cuspy) profile to derive flux predictions, while Paper x (2021) shows that distinguishing a cusp from a core in these same systems remains observationally intractable with current sample sizes—meaning Paper y's underlying density-profile assumption has not yet been empirically verified for the galaxies in question. Additionally, Paper y uses measured velocity dispersion profiles from real data, whereas Paper x uses mock simulated data, so the two studies' claims rest on different methodological bases. The overlapping identification of Ursa Minor and Draco as key targets is consistent across both papers.

x.title: Galactic rotation curves versus ultralight dark matter: Implications of the soliton-host halo relation
x.abstract: Bosonic ultralight dark matter (ULDM) would form cored density distributions at the center of galaxies. These cores, seen in numerical simulations, admit analytic description as the lowest energy bound state solution (``soliton'') of the Schroedinger-Poisson equations. Numerical simulations of ULDM galactic halos find empirical scaling relations between the mass of the large-scale host halo and the mass of the central soliton. We discuss how the simulation results of different groups can be understood in terms of the basic properties of the soliton. Importantly, simulations imply that the energy per unit mass in the soliton and in the virialized host halo should be approximately equal. This relation lends itself to observational tests because it predicts that the peak circular velocity, measured for the host halo in the outskirts of the galaxy, should approximately repeat itself in the central region. Contrasting this prediction with the measured rotation curves of well-resolved nearby galaxies, we show that ULDM in the mass range $m\ensuremath{\sim}({10}^{\ensuremath{-}22}\textdiv{}{10}^{\ensuremath{-}21})\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{eV}$, which has been invoked as a possible solution to the small-scale puzzles of $\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Lambda}}\mathrm{CDM}$, is in tension with the data. We suggest that a dedicated analysis of the Milky Way inner gravitational potential could probe ULDM up to $m\ensuremath{\lesssim}{10}^{\ensuremath{-}19}\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{eV}$.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that ultralight dark matter in the mass range ~10^-22 to 10^-21 eV, proposed to solve small-scale problems of ΛCDM, is in tension with observed galaxy rotation curves.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper tests a specific dark matter candidate (ULDM) by predicting rotation curves from simulated dark matter halo properties, which requires that galaxies are dominated by dark matter (P1) and that Newtonian dynamics correctly describe galactic motions so that rotation curves reflect dark matter halo potentials (P2). If either were rejected—e.g., under MOND—rotation curves would not be interpreted as evidence for dark matter halos and the constraint would be moot.
tag.evidence_quote: Contrasting this prediction with the measured rotation curves of well-resolved nearby galaxies, we show that ULDM in the mass range $m\ensuremath{\sim}({10}^{\ensuremath{-}22}\textdiv{}{10}^{\ensuremath{-}21})\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{eV}$, which has been invoked as a possible solution to the small-scale puzzles of $\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Lambda}}\mathrm{CDM}$, is in tension with the data.

y.title: Axion dark matter, solitons and the cusp–core problem
y.abstract: Self-gravitating bosonic fields can support stable and localized (solitonic) field configurations. Such solitons should be ubiquitous in models of axion dark matter, with their characteristic mass and size depending on some inverse power of the axion mass, ma. Using a scaling symmetry and the uncertainty principle, the soliton core size can be related to the central density and axion mass in a universal way. Solitons have a constant central density due to pressure support, unlike the cuspy profile of cold dark matter (CDM). Consequently, solitons composed of ultralight axions (ULAs) may resolve the ‘cusp–core’ problem of CDM. In dark matter (DM) haloes, thermodynamics will lead to a CDM-like Navarro–Frenk–White (NFW) profile at large radii, with a central soliton core at small radii. Using Monte Carlo techniques to explore the possible density profiles of this form, a fit to stellar kinematical data of dwarf spheroidal galaxies is performed. The data favour cores, and show no preference concerning the NFW part of the halo. In order for ULAs to resolve the cusp–core problem (without recourse to baryon feedback, or other astrophysical effects) the axion mass must satisfy ma < 1.1 × 10−22 eV at 95 per cent C.L. However, ULAs with ma ≲ 1 × 10−22 eV are in some tension with cosmological structure formation. An axion solution to the cusp–core problem thus makes novel predictions for future measurements of the epoch of reionization. On the other hand, improved measurements of structure formation could soon impose a Catch 22 on axion/scalar field DM, similar to the case of warm DM.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that ultralight axion dark matter solitons can resolve the cusp–core problem of CDM without baryon feedback, but only if the axion mass is below ~1.1 × 10^-22 eV, which is in tension with cosmological structure formation.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis assumes non-baryonic dark matter (axion DM) dominates galactic haloes (P1, P4) and uses standard Newtonian gravity to derive soliton structure and fit halo density profiles to dwarf spheroidal kinematics (P2). Rejecting dark matter's existence or standard dynamics at galactic scales would eliminate the premise that axion solitons in DM haloes can address the cusp–core problem.
tag.evidence_quote: Solitons have a constant central density due to pressure support, unlike the cuspy profile of cold dark matter (CDM). Consequently, solitons composed of ultralight axions (ULAs) may resolve the 'cusp–core' problem of CDM.

judge.conjunction: Ultralight dark matter faces severe observational constraints on multiple fronts, as [x] showed that axion masses in the range ~10⁻²² to 10⁻²¹ eV are in tension with observed galaxy rotation curves, while [y] demonstrated that resolving the cusp–core problem requires masses below ~1.1 × 10⁻²² eV, which in turn conflicts with cosmological structure formation.
judge.notes: Both papers operate within Framework P (ΛCDM with ultralight dark matter), so no fundamental theoretical conflict exists between the claims. However, the two constraints nearly close the viable parameter space for ultralight axion dark matter: paper y requires ma < 1.1 × 10⁻²² eV to solve cusp–core, while paper x finds tension with rotation curves starting at ~10⁻²² eV, leaving at most a very narrow window. The two papers also probe somewhat different galaxy types (nearby well-resolved galaxies vs. dwarf spheroidals) and use different methodologies, so a strict joint likelihood analysis would be needed to confirm that no viable mass range remains.

x.title: Relativistic gravitation theory for the modified Newtonian dynamics paradigm
x.abstract: The modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) paradigm of Milgrom can boast of a number of successful predictions regarding galactic dynamics; these are made without the assumption that dark matter plays a significant role. MOND requires gravitation to depart from Newtonian theory in the extragalactic regime where dynamical accelerations are small. So far relativistic gravitation theories proposed to underpin MOND have either clashed with the post-Newtonian tests of general relativity, or failed to provide significant gravitational lensing, or violated hallowed principles by exhibiting superluminal scalar waves or an a priori vector field. We develop a relativistic MOND inspired theory which resolves these problems. In it gravitation is mediated by metric, a scalar, and a 4-vector field, all three dynamical. For a simple choice of its free function, the theory has a Newtonian limit for nonrelativistic dynamics with significant acceleration, but a MOND limit when accelerations are small. We calculate the $\ensuremath{\beta}$ and $\ensuremath{\gamma}$ parameterized post-Newtonian coefficients showing them to agree with solar system measurements. The gravitational light deflection by nonrelativistic systems is governed by the same potential responsible for dynamics of particles. To the extent that MOND successfully describes dynamics of a system, the new theory's predictions for lensing by that system's visible matter will agree as well with observations as general relativity's predictions made with a dynamically successful dark halo model. Cosmological models based on the theory are quite similar to those based on general relativity; they predict slow evolution of the scalar field. For a range of initial conditions, this last result makes it easy to rule out superluminal propagation of metric, scalar, and vector waves.

tag.main_claim: Bekenstein shows that a relativistic gravitation theory involving metric, scalar, and vector fields can reproduce MOND phenomenology at low accelerations while passing solar system tests and yielding gravitational lensing consistent with observations.
tag.dependence_explanation: The theory's entire purpose is to provide a relativistic underpinning for MOND, which assumes galaxy dynamics are explained without dark matter (Q1) and that Newtonian dynamics break down below a characteristic acceleration (Q2). If either assumption is rejected, the theory has no motivation and its central claim of reproducing MOND phenomenology is undercut.
tag.evidence_quote: The modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) paradigm of Milgrom can boast of a number of successful predictions regarding galactic dynamics; these are made without the assumption that dark matter plays a significant role. MOND requires gravitation to depart from Newtonian theory in the extragalactic regime where dynamical accelerations are small.

y.title: A Primer to Relativistic MOND Theory
y.abstract: We first review the nonrelativistic Lagrangian theory as a framework for the MOND equation. Obstructions to a relativistic version of it are discussed leading up to TeVeS, a relativistic tensor-vector-scalar field theory which displays both MOND and Newtonian limits. The whys for its particular structure are discussed and its achievements so far are summarized.

tag.main_claim: Bekenstein shows that TeVeS, a relativistic tensor-vector-scalar field theory, provides a consistent relativistic framework that recovers MOND phenomenology in the low-acceleration limit and Newtonian dynamics in the appropriate limit.
tag.dependence_explanation: TeVeS is constructed as a relativistic extension of MOND, whose core premises are that galaxy dynamics can be explained without dark matter (Q1) and that Newtonian dynamics break down below a characteristic acceleration a0 (Q2). If either premise were rejected, the theory's motivation and defining MOND limit would be undercut.
tag.evidence_quote: We first review the nonrelativistic Lagrangian theory as a framework for the MOND equation. Obstructions to a relativistic version of it are discussed leading up to TeVeS, a relativistic tensor-vector-scalar field theory which displays both MOND and Newtonian limits.

judge.conjunction: Bekenstein [x, y] demonstrates that TeVeS, a relativistic tensor-vector-scalar field theory, recovers MOND phenomenology at low accelerations while passing solar system post-Newtonian tests and yielding gravitational lensing consistent with observations.
judge.notes: Both papers are by the same author and describe the same theory: [y] is a pedagogical primer reviewing TeVeS as introduced in [x], not an independent derivation or confirmation. The conjunction could therefore misleadingly imply two separate lines of evidence where there is essentially one. Additionally, both claims are situated within Framework Q (MOND), which itself conflicts with the Lambda-CDM framework (P) on fundamental points—dark matter's existence (P1 vs Q1), Newtonian validity at low accelerations (P2 vs Q2), the origin of galaxy scaling relations (P3 vs Q3), and the nature of cluster mass discrepancies (P4 vs Q4)—so the asserted claims remain contested by proponents of the standard cosmological model.

x.title: DARK MATTER HEATING AND EARLY CORE FORMATION IN DWARF GALAXIES
x.abstract: We present more results from a fully cosmological ΛCDM simulation of a group of isolated dwarf galaxies that has been shown to reproduce the observed stellar mass and cold gas content, resolved star formation histories, and metallicities of dwarfs in the Local Volume. Here we investigate the energetics and timetable of the cusp–core transformation. As suggested by previous work, supernova-driven gas outflows remove dark matter (DM) cusps and create kiloparsec-size cores in all systems having a stellar mass M * > 10 6 M ☉ . The "DM core mass removal efficiency"—dark mass ejected per unit stellar mass—ranges today from a few to a dozen, and increases with decreasing host mass. Because dwarfs form the bulk of their stars prior to redshift 1 and the amount of work required for DM heating and core formation scales approximately as , the unbinding of the DM cusp starts early and the formation of cored profiles is not as energetically onerous as previously claimed. DM particles in the cusp typically migrate to 2–3 core radii after absorbing a few percent of the energy released by supernovae. The present-day slopes of the inner DM mass profiles, Γ ≡ d log M / d log R ≃ 2.5–3, of the simulated "Bashful" and "Doc" dwarfs are similar to those measured in the luminous Fornax and Sculptor dwarf spheroidals. None of the simulated galaxies has a circular velocity profile exceeding 20 km s −1 in the inner 1 kpc, implying that supernova feedback is key to solve the "too-big-to-fail" problem for Milky Way subhalos.

tag.main_claim: Governato et al. show that supernova-driven gas outflows can remove dark matter cusps and create kiloparsec-size cores in dwarf galaxies within ΛCDM, solving the cusp-core and too-big-to-fail problems without modifying gravity.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire mechanism presupposes that non-baryonic dark matter exists and forms cuspy halos (P1), and that standard Newtonian/GR dynamics govern the gravitational potential so that energy injection from supernovae can heat and redistribute DM particles (P2). Without dark matter, there are no cusps to remove; without standard dynamics, the simulated potential wells and feedback energetics would not apply.
tag.evidence_quote: We present more results from a fully cosmological ΛCDM simulation of a group of isolated dwarf galaxies... As suggested by previous work, supernova-driven gas outflows remove dark matter (DM) cusps and create kiloparsec-size cores in all systems having a stellar mass M * > 10 6 M ☉ .

y.title: Forged in fire: cusps, cores and baryons in low-mass dwarf galaxies
y.abstract: We present multiple ultrahigh resolution cosmological hydrodynamic simulations of M⋆ ≃ 104–6.3 Mȯ dwarf galaxies that form within two Mvir = 109.5–10 Mȯ dark matter halo initial conditions. Our simulations rely on the Feedback in Realistic Environments (fire) implementation of star formation feedback and were run with high enough force and mass resolution to directly resolve structure on the ∼200 pc scales. The resultant galaxies sit on the M⋆ versus Mvir relation required to match the Local Group stellar mass function via abundance matching. They have bursty star formation histories and also form with half-light radii and metallicities that broadly match those observed for local dwarfs at the same stellar mass. We demonstrate that it is possible to create a large (∼1 kpc) constant-density dark matter core in a cosmological simulation of an M⋆ ≃ 106.3 Mȯ dwarf galaxy within a typical Mvir = 1010 Mȯ halo – precisely the scale of interest for resolving the ‘too big to fail’ problem. However, these large cores are not ubiquitous and appear to correlate closely with the star formation histories of the dwarfs: dark matter cores are largest in systems that form their stars late (z ≲ 2), after the early epoch of cusp building mergers has ended. Our M⋆ ≃ 104 Mȯ dwarf retains a cuspy dark matter halo density profile that matches that of a dark-matter-only run of the same system. Though ancient, most of the stars in our ultrafaint form after reionization; the ultraviolet field acts mainly to suppress fresh gas accretion, not to boil away gas that is already present in the protodwarf.

tag.main_claim: Onorbe et al. show that baryonic feedback in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations can create large (~1 kpc) dark matter cores in low-mass dwarf galaxies, with core size correlating with star formation history, addressing the 'too big to fail' problem within Lambda-CDM.
tag.dependence_explanation: The simulations are built entirely within the dark matter framework: they assume dwarf galaxies form within dark matter halos (P1) and use standard Newtonian gravity (P2) to model the dynamics. The central claim that feedback redistributes dark matter to create cores requires dark matter to be real and standard dynamics to govern the simulation.
tag.evidence_quote: We present multiple ultrahigh resolution cosmological hydrodynamic simulations of M⋆ ≃ 104–6.3 Mȯ dwarf galaxies that form within two Mvir = 109.5–10 Mȯ dark matter halo initial conditions.

judge.conjunction: Both Governato et al. [x] and Onorbe et al. [y] demonstrate that supernova-driven baryonic feedback in cosmological ΛCDM simulations can transform dark matter cusps into kiloparsec-scale cores in dwarf galaxies, thereby addressing the cusp-core and too-big-to-fail problems without invoking modified gravity.
judge.notes: The conjunction is largely unproblematic since both papers share the ΛCDM framework and reach compatible conclusions about feedback-driven core formation. However, a minor tension exists in their timescales: Governato et al. emphasize that core formation starts early (bulk of stars form before z~1), while Onorbe et al. find the largest cores in systems that form stars late (z≲2), suggesting the timing of star formation relative to cusp-building mergers matters. Additionally, Onorbe et al. note that large cores are not ubiquitous—some ultrafaint dwarfs retain cusps—whereas Governato et al. report core formation in all systems above a stellar mass threshold, which may reflect differences in feedback prescriptions, halo mass ranges, or simulation resolution.

x.title: The ellipticity of galaxy cluster haloes from satellite galaxies and weak lensing
x.abstract: We study the ellipticity of galaxy cluster haloes as characterized by the distribution of cluster galaxies and as measured with weak lensing. We use Monte Carlo simulations of elliptical cluster density profiles to estimate and correct for Poisson noise bias, edge bias and projection effects. We apply our methodology to 10 428 Sloan Digital Sky Survey clusters identified by the redMaPPer algorithm with richness above 20. We find a mean ellipticity =0.271 ± 0.002 (stat) ±0.031 (sys) corresponding to an axis ratio = 0.573 ± 0.002 (stat) ±0.039 (sys). We compare this ellipticity of the satellites to the halo shape, through a stacked lensing measurement using optimal estimators of the lensing quadrupole based on Clampitt and Jain (2016). We find a best-fitting axis ratio of 0.56 ± 0.09 (stat) ±0.03 (sys), consistent with the ellipticity of the satellite distribution. Thus, cluster galaxies trace the shape of the dark matter halo to within our estimated uncertainties. Finally, we restack the satellite and lensing ellipticity measurements along the major axis of the cluster central galaxy's light distribution. From the lensing measurements, we infer a misalignment angle with an root-mean-square of 30° ± 10° when stacking on the central galaxy. We discuss applications of halo shape measurements to test the effects of the baryonic gas and active galactic nucleus feedback, as well as dark matter and gravity. The major improvements in signal-to-noise ratio expected with the ongoing Dark Energy Survey and future surveys from Large Synoptic Survey Telescope, Euclid, and Wide Field Infrared Survey Telescope will make halo shapes a useful probe of these effects.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that cluster galaxies trace the shape of the dark matter halo in galaxy clusters, with consistent ellipticities from satellite galaxy distributions and weak lensing measurements.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's central claim that satellite galaxies trace 'dark matter halo' shapes requires that non-baryonic dark matter exists (P1) and that galaxy cluster lensing mass is dominated by collisionless dark matter (P4). Under MOND, the weak lensing signal would not be interpreted as tracing a collisionless dark matter halo, undercutting the claim.
tag.evidence_quote: Thus, cluster galaxies trace the shape of the dark matter halo to within our estimated uncertainties.

y.title: Constraining the mass distribution of cluster galaxies by weak lensing
y.abstract: Analysing the weak lensing distortions of the images of faint background galaxies provides a means to constrain the average mass distribution of cluster galaxies and potentially to test the extent of their dark matter haloes as a function of the density of their environment. The observable image distortions are a consequence of the interplay between the effects of a global cluster mass distribution and the perturbations resulting from individual cluster galaxies. Starting from a reconstruction of the cluster mass distribution with conventional techniques, we apply a maximum likelihood method to infer the average properties of an ensemble of cluster galaxies. From simulations this approach is found to be reliable as long as the galaxies including their dark matter haloes only contribute a small fraction to the total mass of the system. If their haloes are extended, the galaxies contain a substantial mass fraction. In this case our method is still applicable in the outer regions of clusters, where the surface mass density is low, but yields biased estimates of the parameters describing the mass profiles of the cluster galaxies in the central part of the cluster. In that case it will be necessary to resort to more sophisticated strategies by modelling cluster galaxies and an underlying global mass distribution simultaneously. We conclude that galaxy-galaxy lensing in clusters provides a unique means to probe the presence and extent of dark haloes of cluster galaxies.

tag.main_claim: The paper shows that weak galaxy-galaxy lensing in clusters can constrain the presence and spatial extent of dark matter haloes around cluster galaxies, though with biases in cluster centers when haloes are extended.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's central claim is about probing dark matter haloes of cluster galaxies, which requires that non-baryonic dark matter exists (P1) and that cluster lensing mass is dominated by collisionless dark matter (P4). Without dark matter haloes, the entire methodology and conclusion have no subject to probe.
tag.evidence_quote: We conclude that galaxy-galaxy lensing in clusters provides a unique means to probe the presence and extent of dark haloes of cluster galaxies.

judge.conjunction: Weak lensing has proven a powerful probe of dark matter in galaxy clusters, from early work constraining the presence and spatial extent of galaxy-scale dark haloes within clusters [y] to more recent stacked measurements demonstrating that satellite galaxy distributions faithfully trace the shape of the cluster-scale dark matter halo [x].
judge.notes: Both papers operate within Framework P (Lambda-CDM), so no theoretical conflict arises. However, the two claims operate at different mass scales: Paper y concerns individual galaxy haloes within clusters (galaxy-galaxy lensing), while Paper x concerns the overall cluster halo shape (stacked cluster lensing). Conflating these scales in a single narrative risks implying they measure the same thing. Additionally, Paper y explicitly notes that its method yields biased estimates in cluster centers when galaxy haloes are extended, a caveat that could bear on the central-region shape measurements in Paper x but is not addressed there. The 20-year gap between the papers also entails very different survey data quality and methodology, which the sentence smooths over.

x.title: MOND theory
x.abstract: A general account of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) theory is given. I start with the basic tenets of MOND, which posit departure from standard dynamics in the limit of low acceleration — below an acceleration constant a0 — where dynamics become scale invariant. I list some of the salient predictions of these tenets. The special role of a0 and its significance are then discussed. In particular, I stress its coincidence with cosmologically relevant accelerations, which may point to MOND having deep interplay with cosmology. The deep-MOND limit and the consequences of its scale invariance are considered in some detail. There are many ways to achieve scale invariance of the equations of motion — guaranteed if the total action has a well-defined scaling dimension. The mere realization that this is enough to ensure MOND phenomenology opens a wide scope for constructing MOND theories. General aspects of MOND theories are then described, after which I list briefly presently known theories, both nonrelativistic and relativistic. With few exceptions, the construction of known, full-fledged theories follows the same rough pattern: they modify the gravitational action; hinge on a0; introduce, already at the level of the action, an interpolating function between the low and high accelerations; and they obey MOND requirements in the two opposite limits. These theories have much heuristic value as proofs of various concepts (e.g., that covariant MOND theories can be written with correct gravitational lensing). But, probably, none points to the final MOND theory. At best, they are effective theories of limited applicability. I argue that we have so far explored only a small corner of the space of possible MOND theories. I then outline several other promising approaches to constructing MOND theories that strive to obtain MOND as an effective theory from deeper concepts, for example, by modifying inertia and (or) gravity as a result of interactions with some omnipresent agent. These have made encouraging progress in various degrees, but have not yet resulted in full-fledged theories that can be applied to all systems and situations. Some of the presently known theories do enjoy a natural appearance of a cosmological-constant-like contribution that, furthermore, exhibits the observed connection with a0. However, none were shown to address fully the mass discrepancies in cosmology and structure formation that are otherwise explained by cosmological dark matter. This may well be due to our present ignorance of the true connections between MOND and cosmology. We have no clues as to whether and how MOND aspects enter nongravitational phenomena, but I discuss briefly some possibilities.

tag.main_claim: Milgrom reviews MOND theory and shows that its basic tenets—departure from standard dynamics below acceleration a0 and scale invariance in the deep-MOND limit—open a wide scope for constructing modified gravity theories that reproduce MOND phenomenology including correct gravitational lensing, though no complete theory yet addresses all cosmological mass discrepancies.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's entire theoretical program rests on MOND's core claims: that galaxy dynamics need no dark matter (Q1), that Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2), and that scaling relations follow from the modified force law (Q3). Rejecting any of these would eliminate the foundation on which the constructions and predictions described in the paper are built.
tag.evidence_quote: I start with the basic tenets of MOND, which posit departure from standard dynamics in the limit of low acceleration — below an acceleration constant a0 — where dynamics become scale invariant. I list some of the salient predictions of these tenets.

y.title: MOND laws of galactic dynamics
y.abstract: Modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) predicts a number of laws that galactic systems should obey irrespective of their complicated, haphazard and mostly unknowable histories – as Kepler's laws are obeyed by planetary systems. The main purpose of this work is to show how, and to what extent, these MOND laws follow from only the paradigm's basic tenets: departure from standard dynamics at accelerations a ≲ a0 and space–time scale invariance in the limit a ≪ a0. Such predictions will be shared by all MOND theories that embody these premises. This is important because we do not know which of the existing MOND theories, if any, is a step in the right direction. In the Newtonian dynamics plus dark matter paradigm, the validity of such clear-cut laws – which tightly constrain baryons, ‘dark matter’ and their mutual relations – is contrary to expectations.

tag.main_claim: Milgrom shows that MOND predicts clear-cut laws of galactic dynamics that follow directly from the paradigm's basic tenets—modified dynamics at low accelerations and space-time scale invariance—akin to how Kepler's laws follow from Newtonian gravity.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's claim that galactic dynamical laws follow from MOND tenets requires that galaxy dynamics be explained without dark matter (Q1), that Newtonian dynamics break down below a0 (Q2, explicitly cited as a basic tenet), and that scaling relations derive from the force law rather than from galaxy formation (Q3).
tag.evidence_quote: The main purpose of this work is to show how, and to what extent, these MOND laws follow from only the paradigm's basic tenets: departure from standard dynamics at accelerations a ≲ a0 and space–time scale invariance in the limit a ≪ a0.

judge.conjunction: Milgrom [x, y] demonstrates that MOND's basic tenets—departure from standard dynamics below the acceleration constant a0 and space-time scale invariance in the deep-MOND limit—not only yield clear-cut, Kepler-like laws of galactic dynamics that follow directly from these premises, but also open a wide scope for constructing modified gravity theories that reproduce MOND phenomenology including correct gravitational lensing, though no complete theory yet addresses all cosmological mass discrepancies.
judge.notes: Both papers are by the same author (Milgrom) and within the same framework (MOND), so the claims are complementary rather than conflicting. Minor concern: the 'basic tenets' are described slightly differently across the two claims—Claim X emphasizes scale invariance of the action/equations of motion, while Claim Y emphasizes space-time scale invariance—which are related but not identical formulations, so the literature-review writer should verify that the merged phrasing is precise enough. Additionally, the juxtaposition of strong predictive success (Kepler-like laws) with the acknowledged failure to address cosmological mass discrepancies could invite a reader to question the overall viability of the paradigm, though this is an internal tension within MOND rather than a contradiction between the two claims.

x.title: Novel Test of Modified Newtonian Dynamics with Gas Rich Galaxies
x.abstract: The current cosmological paradigm, the cold dark matter model with a cosmological constant, requires that the mass-energy of the Universe be dominated by invisible components: dark matter and dark energy. An alternative to these dark components is that the law of gravity be modified on the relevant scales. A test of these ideas is provided by the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation (BTFR), an empirical relation between the observed mass of a galaxy and its rotation velocity. Here, I report a test using gas rich galaxies for which both axes of the BTFR can be measured independently of the theories being tested and without the systematic uncertainty in stellar mass that affects the same test with star dominated spirals. The data fall precisely where predicted a priori by the modified Newtonian dynamics. The scatter in the BTFR is attributable entirely to observational uncertainty, consistent with a single effective force law.

tag.main_claim: McGaugh shows that gas-rich galaxies fall precisely on the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation with scatter attributable entirely to observational uncertainty, consistent with a single effective force law governing galaxy dynamics.
tag.dependence_explanation: The claim depends on MOND's modified force law (Q2) producing a specific, a priori prediction for the BTFR normalization and slope (Q3). If Newtonian dynamics held at low accelerations, or if the BTFR emerged from galaxy formation physics rather than a fundamental force law, MOND's prediction would not be the thing being validated.
tag.evidence_quote: The data fall precisely where predicted a priori by the modified Newtonian dynamics. The scatter in the BTFR is attributable entirely to observational uncertainty, consistent with a single effective force law.

y.title: Fitting the radial acceleration relation to individual SPARC galaxies
y.abstract: Galaxies follow a tight radial acceleration relation (RAR): the acceleration observed at every radius correlates with that expected from the distribution of baryons. We use the Markov chain Monte Carlo method to fit the mean RAR to 175 individual galaxies in the SPARC database, marginalizing over stellar mass-to-light ratio (ϒ⋆), galaxy distance, and disk inclination. Acceptable fits with astrophysically reasonable parameters are found for the vast majority of galaxies. The residuals around these fits have an rms scatter of only 0.057 dex (~13%). This is in agreement with the predictions of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND). We further consider a generalized version of the RAR that, unlike MOND, permits galaxy-to-galaxy variation in the critical acceleration scale. The fits are not improved with this additional freedom: there is no credible indication of variation in the critical acceleration scale. The data are consistent with the action of a single effective force law. The apparent universality of the acceleration scale and the small residual scatter are key to understanding galaxies.

tag.main_claim: The radial acceleration relation across 175 SPARC galaxies shows a universal critical acceleration scale with only ~13% residual scatter, consistent with a single effective force law as predicted by MOND.
tag.dependence_explanation: The paper's claim that the RAR reflects a single effective force law with a universal critical acceleration scale directly invokes MOND's core tenets: that baryons alone explain galaxy dynamics (Q1), that dynamics break down below a characteristic acceleration a0 (Q2), and that scaling relations like the RAR follow directly from the force law rather than from galaxy formation (Q3). If any of these were rejected—for instance, if the RAR arose from dark matter halo physics (P3) rather than a fundamental force law—the paper's central interpretive conclusion would be undercut.
tag.evidence_quote: This is in agreement with the predictions of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND). We further consider a generalized version of the RAR that, unlike MOND, permits galaxy-to-galaxy variation in the critical acceleration scale. The fits are not improved with this additional freedom: there is no credible indication of variation in the critical acceleration scale. The data are consistent with the action of a single effective force law.

judge.conjunction: Multiple lines of evidence support the existence of a single effective force law governing galaxy dynamics: gas-rich galaxies fall precisely on the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation with scatter attributable entirely to observational uncertainty [x], and the radial acceleration relation across 175 SPARC galaxies exhibits a universal critical acceleration scale with only ~13% residual scatter, both consistent with MOND predictions [y].
judge.notes: Both papers operate within MOND (Framework Q) and make mutually reinforcing claims, so no framework-level conflict arises. However, potential concerns include: (1) author overlap—McGaugh is a coauthor on both papers, weakening the appearance of independent confirmation; (2) the BTFR (Paper x) and RAR (Paper y) are distinct empirical relations—a global mass-velocity scaling and a local acceleration-acceleration correlation, respectively—so treating them as two independent tests of the same law slightly conflates different observables; (3) Paper x's stronger claim that BTFR scatter is 'entirely' observational is not identically phrased in Paper y, which reports ~13% rms scatter 'in agreement with' MOND without asserting it is fully observational in origin.

x.title: Diversity of Dark Matter Density Profiles in the Galactic Dwarf Spheroidal Satellites
x.abstract: Abstract The core–cusp problem is one of the controversial issues in the standard paradigm of Λ cold dark matter (ΛCDM) theory. However, under the assumption of conventional spherical symmetry, the strong degeneracy among model parameters makes it unclear whether dwarf spheroidal (dSph) galaxies indeed have cored dark matter density profiles at their centers. In this work, we revisit this problem using nonspherical mass models, which have the advantage of being able to alleviate the degeneracy. Applying our mass models to the currently available kinematic data of the eight classical dSphs, we find that within finite uncertainties, most of these dSphs favor cusped central profiles rather than cored ones. In particular, Draco has a cusped dark matter halo with high probability even considering a prior bias. We also find the diversity of the inner slopes in their dark matter halos. To clarify the origin of this diversity, we investigate the relation between the inner dark matter density slope and stellar-to-halo mass ratio for the sample dSphs and find that this relation is generally in agreement with the predictions from recent ΛCDM and hydrodynamical simulations. We also find that the simulated subhalos have an anticorrelation between the dark matter density at 150 pc and pericenter distance, which is consistent with the observed one. We estimate their astrophysical factors for dark matter indirect searches and circular velocity profiles associated with huge uncertainties. To more precisely estimate their dark matter profiles, wide-field spectroscopic surveys for the dSphs are essential.

tag.main_claim: Hayashi et al. show that most classical dwarf spheroidal galaxies favor cusped dark matter density profiles, and that the diversity of inner slopes is consistent with ΛCDM hydrodynamical simulations.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis presupposes that dwarf spheroidals are dominated by non-baryonic dark matter halos (P1) and uses Newtonian Jeans modeling to infer mass profiles from stellar kinematic data (P2). If dark matter did not exist or if dynamics were modified at low accelerations, the inferred density profiles and their cusped nature would not follow.
tag.evidence_quote: we find that within finite uncertainties, most of these dSphs favor cusped central profiles rather than cored ones... this relation is generally in agreement with the predictions from recent ΛCDM and hydrodynamical simulations.

y.title: DARK AND LUMINOUS MATTER IN THINGS DWARF GALAXIES
y.abstract: We present mass models for the dark matter component of seven dwarf galaxies taken from "The H i Nearby Galaxy Survey" (THINGS) and compare these with those taken from numerical Λ cold dark matter (ΛCDM) simulations. The THINGS high-resolution data significantly reduce observational uncertainties and thus allow us to derive accurate dark matter distributions in these systems. We here use the bulk velocity fields when deriving the rotation curves of the galaxies. Compared to other types of velocity fields, the bulk velocity field minimizes the effect of small-scale random motions more effectively and traces the underlying kinematics of a galaxy more properly. The " Spitzer Infrared Nearby Galaxies Survey" 3.6 μm and ancillary optical data are used for separating the baryons from their total matter content in the galaxies. The sample dwarf galaxies are found to be dark matter dominated over most radii. The relation between total baryonic (stars + gas) mass and maximum rotation velocity of the galaxies is roughly consistent with the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation calibrated from a larger sample of gas-dominated low-mass galaxies. We find discrepancies between the derived dark matter distributions of the galaxies and those of ΛCDM simulations, even after corrections for non-circular motions have been applied. The observed solid body-like rotation curves of the galaxies rise too slowly to reflect the cusp-like dark matter distribution in cold dark matter halos. Instead, they are better described by core-like models such as pseudo-isothermal halo models dominated by a central constant-density core. The mean value of the logarithmic inner slopes of the mass density profiles is α = −0.29 ± 0.07. They are significantly different from the steep slope of ∼ − 1.0 inferred from previous dark-matter-only simulations, and are more consistent with shallower slopes found in recent ΛCDM simulations of dwarf galaxies in which the effects of baryonic feedback processes are included.

tag.main_claim: Oh et al. show that THINGS dwarf galaxies have core-like dark matter distributions with shallow inner density slopes (α ≈ −0.29), inconsistent with dark-matter-only ΛCDM simulations but more consistent with ΛCDM simulations including baryonic feedback.
tag.dependence_explanation: The entire analysis assumes dark matter exists and dominates the mass budget of these galaxies (P1), and uses Newtonian dynamics to infer mass distributions from rotation curves (P2). Rejecting either would invalidate the premise that the measured mass discrepancies correspond to actual dark matter halos.
tag.evidence_quote: The sample dwarf galaxies are found to be dark matter dominated over most radii.

judge.conjunction: Within the ΛCDM framework, dwarf galaxy dark matter profiles have been shown to span a diversity of inner slopes—from cusped profiles in classical dwarf spheroidals consistent with hydrodynamical simulations [x] to core-like profiles in THINGS dwarfs with shallow slopes more consistent with feedback-inclusive than dark-matter-only simulations [y].
judge.notes: The conjunction papers over a genuine cusp–core tension: Hayashi et al. find that most classical dSphs favor cusped profiles, whereas Oh et al. find core-like profiles in THINGS dwarfs. While both invoke ΛCDM with baryonic feedback, the two results pull in opposite directions regarding the typical inner structure of dwarf dark matter halos. The studies also use different galaxy populations (kinematically modeled Milky Way satellites vs. gas-rich, rotationally supported field dwarfs) and different methods (stellar kinematics with nonspherical mass models vs. H I rotation curves), so a direct comparison is not straightforward, and framing them as a smooth 'diversity' may oversimplify the disagreement.

x.title: The dark and visible matter content of low surface brightness disc galaxies
x.abstract: We present mass models of a sample of 19 low surface brightness (LSB) galaxies and compare the properties of their constituent mass components with those of a sample of high surface brightness (HSB) galaxies. We find that LSB galaxies are dark matter dominated. Their halo parameters are only slightly affected by assumptions on stellar mass-to-light ratios. Comparing LSB and HSB galaxies we find that mass models derived using the maximum disc hypothesis result in the discs of LSB galaxies having systematically higher stellar mass-to-light ratios than HSB galaxies of similar rotation velocity.
